entries.narration: Every algorithm in this course starts from a problem, so it is worth being precise about what a problem is. A problem says what answer every possible input deserves. An instance is one particular input. Our running example is a small delivery planner. It keeps a list of parcels, each with an identifier such as P three-seventeen, and the first problem is lookup: given the list and an identifier, say where that parcel is. At the top of the board are three instances: four parcels with a target that is present, the same parcels with a target that is absent, and an empty list. Each has exactly one required output, and an algorithm solves the problem only if it is right on all of them, the awkward ones included. The required outputs are pinned down by a specification, which is best read as a contract with two sides. The caller makes the first promise, the precondition: a finite list of parcel records, each with a string identifier. The function makes the second, the postcondition: it returns the least index whose identifier matches the target, or None if there is none, and it leaves the list unchanged. With both written down, correct has an exact meaning. Whenever the precondition holds, the postcondition must hold afterwards, on every instance. If a caller breaks the precondition, the contract promises nothing at all. The awkward instances are where the contract has to make real choices. When two records share an identifier, or the target is missing, there are several reasonable rules, shown at the bottom. Return the first match. Return every match. Or insist that identifiers are unique and raise an error otherwise. Each rule changes the work as well as the answer: first match can stop at the first hit, while all matches must always inspect the whole list. In this chapter we use first match, with None for a missing target.

Requests arrive in everyday language. A dispatcher at the North depot asks, where is parcel P three-seventeen? Before we can compute anything, that question has to become a model, which is a deliberate simplification that keeps only what the computation needs. Our model has three parts. The data is a list of parcel records. The query is one identifier string. The answer is a position in the list, or None. Just as important is what the model leaves out: scanners, trucks and the time of day. They are real, but they do not affect this lookup, so we drop them on purpose and write the omission down. Many problems ask for more than one right answer. They ask for the best of many acceptable ones, and two ideas keep those problems clear. A constraint decides which answers are allowed at all, and the allowed answers form the feasible set. An objective then ranks the feasible answers. For the question, which is the lightest parcel at North, being at North is the constraint and weight is the objective. The same situation can be asked as a decision, is there a North parcel under three kilograms, as a search, find one, or as an optimisation, find the lightest. Those forms differ a great deal in difficulty for harder problems, as the final chapter shows. Finally, no claim about an algorithm stands on its own. It holds under assumptions, and the bottom of the board names ours. Identifiers are compared exactly, so a lowercase p or a trailing space is a miss. Nobody edits the list during the search, because an index found a moment ago can go stale. Comparing two identifiers counts as one step, which is fair for short strings but not long ones. And the data is in memory, never waiting on a disk or a network. The reason to state them is that a broken assumption rarely announces itself. The code still runs. It just stops meaning what we said it meant.

Before reaching for anything clever, write a baseline: the simplest solution you can convince yourself is correct. It earns its place through what it does afterwards. It is a test oracle, because any faster version can be checked against it on many inputs. It is a specification check, because writing even a simple solution forces unclear cases, like the empty list, into the open. And it is a yardstick, the cost a cleverer idea has to beat on real inputs before it is worth its complexity. For lookup, the baseline is the obvious one: look at each parcel in turn, and stop at the first match. The top card states it in pseudocode, a way of writing an algorithm without committing to one language. This course keeps a few conventions. Indices start at zero, as in Python. A left arrow means assignment and a single equals sign means comparison, so the two cannot be confused. A loop from zero to n minus one includes both ends. And the contract sits on top as comments. Pseudocode matters even though Python reads almost like it, because Python hides work. A slice or an in test can copy or scan a whole list without saying so, while in pseudocode every line on the page is a step the algorithm actually takes. The middle card is the Python translation, line for line, with the postcondition kept as the docstring. Because the indices are visited in increasing order, the first match is also the least. The bottom card is what the file actually printed under CPython three point one four. Looking up P three-seventeen gives two. An absent identifier gives None, and so does the empty list, whose loop body never runs. One design choice deserves a word. Many languages signal not found with minus one. In Python that is dangerous, because minus one is a valid index meaning the last element. None cannot be used as an index by mistake.

To reason about a running program, we need a precise picture of where it is. That picture is the state: every name in scope and the value it refers to, at one moment. Inside our loop, the list and the target never change during the call. Only i moves, and expressions like parcels at i dot pid are derived from the rest. Each step of the program turns one state into the next, and a trace is simply the sequence of states in order. The script on the board is the baseline, instrumented to print its own state. The trick is to record the same point in every iteration, and to print before acting on the comparison, so that even the iteration that returns leaves a line. Searching for P three-seventeen, the output shows indices zero and one inspected and rejected. Index two matches, and the function returns two straight away. Notice what is missing. Index three was never inspected, which means the cost of a lookup depends on where the target sits, not only on how long the list is. The next chapter turns that observation into analysis. The cases that find nothing deserve traces of their own, because they take a different path. The tables at the bottom are traced by hand. With an absent target, every index is inspected, every comparison is false, nothing inside the loop returns, and control falls through to the final line, which returns None. An empty list is shorter still. A range of length zero produces no values, so the body runs zero times, and the very same final line answers. Two quite different instances reach one return statement for the same reason: no index matched. In any trace, two questions catch most mistakes. Which was the last index actually inspected? And which line produced the result?

A trace tells us what happened in one run. To say something about every run, we need a loop invariant: a statement that is true every time execution reaches a chosen point, here the top of each iteration. For our baseline the invariant is: the target is not in the part of the list before index i. The board shows a search for P four-fifty-eight at i equals two. The first two parcels have been inspected and rejected, which is exactly what the invariant says, and the rest are still unknown. An invariant is only useful if it can be checked, and the three checks together form an argument by induction on i. Initialisation is the base case. When the loop starts, i is zero, the prefix is empty, and an empty prefix cannot contain the target. Maintenance is the inductive step. Suppose the invariant holds at some i. If the body does not return, the parcel at i did not match, so there is still no match up to and including i, and the invariant holds for i plus one. Exit is where we collect. If the loop finishes without returning, i has reached n, the length of the list, so no index matches, and returning None is exactly what the postcondition requires. The same reasoning covers the early return: when the function returns i, nothing before i matched, so i is the least matching index. There is still a gap. The invariant proves the answer is right if the loop stops. Termination needs its own proof, and the standard technique is a decreasing measure: a whole number that falls on every iteration and can never drop below zero. Here it is n minus i, the parcels not yet inspected. It starts at n and falls by one each time, so the loop runs at most n times. The range object makes this nearly automatic. A hand-written while loop is where it really matters, since one missing increment turns a correct loop into an endless one. Keep one distinction: proving the loop stops says nothing about how fast it stops. That is the next chapter's question.

A claim that a function works for every valid input is a universal claim, and a single instance where it fails refutes it. That instance is called a counterexample. The function on the board contains a very plausible bug. Someone has added an else branch that returns None as soon as one parcel fails to match. It passes all three of its tests. The target at the front is found, and the two absent targets correctly give None. And yet the last line of output shows the function is wrong: P three-seventeen, which sits at index two, comes back as None. The invariant argument explains exactly why. Maintenance needs every rejected index to be followed by another iteration, but this version stops after rejecting index zero and announces that nothing matches anywhere. The tests missed it because none of them had a target beyond the first position, so none of them reached the faulty path. Bugs cluster at the edges of the input space, so boundary cases should be chosen on purpose rather than hoped for. For algorithms over sequences, the checklist is short: an empty input and a single item; the target first, last and absent; and duplicates, where the contract decides which match wins. Run against our baseline, every case agrees with the contract. One more boundary sits on the caller's side. Index zero is a perfectly good answer, but in Python zero counts as false in a condition. A caller who writes, if i, treats a parcel found at the very front as not found. Test the result with, is not None, which says exactly what the contract means. It helps to be exact about how far each kind of evidence reaches. Passing tests show correctness on the inputs they ran, and on nothing else. A proof covers every input that meets the precondition, including the infinitely many nobody will try. And one counterexample shows a universal claim is false, however many tests passed before it. They work together. Tests catch slips in a proof and in its translation to code, and a proof explains why the tested cases pass.

The last part of this chapter is about how Python represents data, because several later arguments depend on it. In Python a variable is a name, and a name refers to an object. Assigning one name to another never copies anything. Writing route equals today just gives the same list a second name, so appending through route changes what today sees. This sharing is called aliasing, and it is how a function that promised to leave a list unchanged can still find it changed, by some other part of the program holding another name for it. To get an independent list you copy, and there are two kinds of copy. The script on the board makes both. A shallow copy, made with the copy method, builds a new list but fills it with references to the same parcel objects. A deep copy, made with copy dot deepcopy, builds new parcel objects as well. The output and the object graph show the difference. Appending to the shallow copy leaves the original at length one, because the two lists really are separate. But changing the original parcel's depot to South shows through the shallow copy, since both lists hold the very same parcel. Only the deep copy still says North. Copying also has a cost that is easy to miss. A shallow copy of n items is linear work, and a deep copy also copies everything it can reach. Numbers carry assumptions too. Integers are exact, which is why the planner stores weights in whole grams. Floating point numbers round, so adding nought point one to a total ten times gives a value just short of one. Since CPython three point one two the built-in sum function compensates for that rounding, but that is a detail of one implementation, so no algorithm should rely on it. The double slash operator floors towards minus infinity, so minus seven floor-divided by two is minus four. And Python integers have no fixed size. Two to the power two hundred is exact, but arithmetic on huge numbers is no longer a single step, which the next chapter makes precise.

Chapter one ended with a correct lookup. This chapter asks how much it costs, and the first step is to agree on what we are counting. That agreement is called a cost model, and it fixes three things. First, the input size. For a list of parcels it is usually the number of items, n. For a single number it should be the number of digits or bits needed to write it down. Second, what counts as one step: an operation we charge a constant cost, such as comparing two identifiers or adding two machine-size numbers. Third, what we count: steps, memory, or both, as a function of the input size. These choices matter most when the input is a single value rather than a collection. The script on the board finds the smallest factor of a number by trial division. It tries divisors up to the square root of n, so it takes about root n steps. Measured against the value n, that sounds modest. But look at the output. Each time the number gains two digits, n is a hundred times larger, and the step count is ten times larger. Two digits, eight steps. Eight digits, nearly ten thousand. Against the true input size, the number of digits, the cost is exponential. A two hundred digit number would need more steps than any computer could ever take. The same algorithm is polynomial in the value and exponential in the encoding, and only the second description is honest about how hard the problem is. This distinction returns in the dynamic programming chapter. Finally, charging one unit per operation is itself an assumption. It is fair for short identifiers and numbers that fit in a machine word. It is not fair for very long strings or for Python's arbitrary-size integers, where the work grows with the length. Every cost claim in this course states which kind of operation it treats as one step.

With a cost model agreed, the next skill is counting. The advice here is simple and easy to skip: count the steps first, and only afterwards choose a notation to summarise them. The script on the board instruments two computations on the same list of identifiers. The first is our lookup with a target that is absent, so it compares the target with every parcel once, n comparisons in all. The second checks whether any two parcels share an identifier, by comparing every pair exactly once. Its inner loop starts at i plus one, so the first parcel is compared with n minus one others, the next with n minus two, and so on down to zero. That sum is n times n minus one over two. A few rules cover most code. Steps that happen one after another add. A loop multiplies the cost of its body by the number of times it runs. When the inner loop's length depends on the outer index, as here, the honest count is a sum, and the sum is worth writing out before simplifying it. Constant work inside each iteration, like incrementing a counter, is counted too, and only simplified away later. The output shows why the distinction matters. As n doubles from four to eight to sixteen to thirty-two, the lookup count doubles each time. The all-pairs count goes six, twenty-eight, one hundred and twenty, four hundred and ninety-six, roughly four times larger at each step. At four parcels the two computations are close. At a million parcels, the first takes a million comparisons and the second about half a trillion. That gap, which appears only as n grows, is exactly what the notation in the next section is designed to capture.

Exact counts are precise but awkward to compare. Asymptotic notation keeps what matters for large inputs, the growth rate, and drops constant factors and small terms. There are three bounds. A function f is big O of g if, from some point n nought onwards, f is at most a constant times g. That is an upper bound. f is big Omega of g if, from some point on, f is at least a constant times g. That is a lower bound. And f is big Theta of g if both hold, so that g describes the growth rate exactly, up to constants. The plot shows this for a cost function of three n plus five. From n equals five onwards, it stays between the line three n below and the line four n above. Squeezed between two constant multiples of n, it is Theta of n. Notice that the constants and the starting point are part of the claim. Choosing them is how you prove a bound. One distinction causes more confusion than any other in this topic. A bound is not a case. Before applying any notation, you must decide which function you are describing. For lookup there are several. The worst-case cost, the most steps over all inputs of size n, is n, so the worst case is Theta of n. The best-case cost, with the target at the front, is one step, so the best case is Theta of one. Both are perfectly precise statements. The popular phrase, big O means the worst case, mixes the two ideas together. Big O is an upper bound on whatever function you chose, and the worst case is one choice of function. You can give an upper bound on the best case, or a lower bound on the worst case, and both are sometimes exactly what an argument needs. The most useful single statement is usually an upper bound on the worst case, because it covers every input.

An algorithm does not have one cost. It has a cost for every input, and analysis needs a principled way to turn all of those into a single number. There are three common ways, and each rests on a different assumption. The worst case takes the maximum over all inputs of a given size. For lookup over one hundred parcels, an absent target costs one hundred comparisons, and no input of that size costs more. The worst case assumes nothing about the input, which is why it is a guarantee. The average case takes a weighted mean over a stated distribution of inputs. If every present target is equally likely, the cost of finding the parcel at position k is k, and the mean over all positions is n plus one over two, which is fifty point five, exactly what the script computes. The average is only as good as the distribution behind it. If dispatchers mostly ask about recent parcels, stored at the end, the real average is close to the worst case. The script also estimates the average with a random sample of a thousand targets, using a fixed seed so the run is repeatable. The estimate, fifty-one point nine, is close but not equal. A sample estimates an expectation. It does not compute it. The third kind is expected cost in the stronger sense: averaged over random choices the algorithm makes itself, such as a random pivot in quicksort later on. That expectation holds for every input, because the randomness belongs to the algorithm, not to the data. The difference matters when inputs might be chosen against you. An adversary can pick the input that triggers your worst case. It cannot pick your coin flips.

A small family of functions describes almost every algorithm in this course, and it pays to know them by shape. The plot shows them on one pair of axes, and the printed table gives exact values. The logarithm grows slowest. Log base two of n counts how many times n can be halved before one is left, so log two of sixty-four is six. Any algorithm that throws away half of its remaining work at each step, such as binary search, costs a logarithm. Next come n, one pass over the input, and n log n, the cost of good sorting algorithms, which in practice behaves almost like n. Then n squared, the cost of looking at every pair, which we met in the duplicate check. And finally two to the n, the number of subsets of n items, which is the cost of trying every combination. At sixty-four items, two to the n already has twenty digits. On the plot it leaves the chart before n reaches eight. A note on logarithms. Changing the base, say from two to ten, only multiplies the value by a constant. That is why asymptotic statements usually write log n without a base. The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms, so the log of n squared is just twice log n, still Theta of log n. And it grows very slowly indeed: a million items need only about twenty halvings. Two sums appear again and again. The sum of one up to n is n times n plus one over two, which is Theta of n squared. The script checks it at a hundred: five thousand and fifty both ways. The geometric sum one plus two plus four, up to two to the k, equals two to the k plus one, minus one. Here the last term alone is more than half of the total. That fact will explain why doubling a dynamic array costs only constant time per append on average, and why a heap can be built in linear time.

When a function calls itself, its cost is naturally defined in terms of itself. Such a definition is called a recurrence, and the most reliable way to solve one is to draw the calls it makes. Consider two shapes of recursion. The first makes one call on half of its input, like binary search. Its cost is T of n equals T of n over two, plus one, with T of one equal to one. Each call does constant work and passes half the input down, so the calls form a single path, of length about log base two of n, plus one. In the output, an input of twenty-five needs only five calls. The second shape makes two calls on slightly smaller inputs, like the naive Fibonacci function. Its recurrence is T of n equals T of n minus one, plus T of n minus two, plus one. Now the calls form a tree, drawn on the board for an input of four. Each level of that tree can hold up to twice as many calls as the level above, so the total grows exponentially. For an input of twenty-five, the program makes two hundred and forty-two thousand, seven hundred and eighty-five calls. The tree also shows why. The call for two, highlighted, appears twice already at this small size, and its whole subtree is recomputed each time. That repetition is the waste that dynamic programming will remove, by solving each subproblem once and remembering the answer. The general method is called recursion-tree reasoning. Draw the tree of calls. Write the work done at each node, not counting its children. Total the work level by level. Then add up the levels. For the halving recursion, every level costs one, and there are log n levels. For the branching one, the levels grow geometrically, and the last level dominates.

Time is not the only resource an algorithm consumes. Memory matters too, and it helps to divide it into kinds. Input space and output space are fixed by the problem itself. What an algorithm controls is auxiliary space: the extra memory it needs while it runs, such as temporary lists, tables or a queue. One kind of auxiliary space is easy to forget. Every call that has started but not yet returned holds a stack frame with its arguments and local variables, so the depth of recursion costs memory in proportion to that depth. The script compares two recursive functions that both add up a list. The first looks elegant. It adds the first item to the sum of the rest, where the rest is the slice x s from one onwards. But a slice in Python is a new list, so every call copies everything after the first element. For five hundred items, the script counts one hundred and twenty-four thousand, seven hundred and fifty elements copied. That is about n squared over two, Theta of n squared work and allocation, for a computation that should be linear. The second version passes the same list together with an index, and copies nothing. Both versions, though, recurse once per element, so both keep n stack frames alive at the deepest point. Python bounds that depth. CPython's default recursion limit is one thousand, and the last line shows what happens at five thousand: the call raises a recursion error instead of returning a slow answer. So for long sequences, a recursive formulation needs either a loop or an explicit stack. Chapter eight returns to this. The lesson for analysis is to count the hidden costs: copies made by slicing, objects allocated per call, and the depth of the call stack.

Analysis predicts how cost grows. Measurement checks whether the prediction shows up on a real machine, and explains the part that analysis deliberately throws away. The script times two ways of searching for an absent identifier: our hand-written loop, and Python's built-in in operator. Both are linear searches, so both are Theta of n. The card shows one recorded run on this container, and it is labelled that way on purpose, because a second run gives different numbers. Several things are visible. Doubling n roughly doubles the loop's time, as the analysis predicts. The built-in is about two times faster at every size. That is a difference in the constant factor, which asymptotic notation hides on purpose, and which can decide between two algorithms of the same growth rate. And the built-in's time more than doubles between one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand items. That comes from effects the cost model ignores entirely, such as how the list's data fits in the processor's caches. Good measurement takes some care. Repeat each run several times and keep the minimum, because the noise comes from other work on the machine, not from the algorithm. Change one thing at a time. State the machine, the Python version, and the input sizes, so others can compare. And remember what a timing can and cannot show. It is evidence about the inputs you timed, on the machine you timed them on. It proves nothing about larger inputs, other data, or another interpreter. That is why the order in this course is fixed. First a correct algorithm, then an analysis under a stated model, and only then benchmarks, to check the analysis and to choose between candidates whose growth rates are equal.

This chapter is about sequences, and it starts with the most basic representation of all, the array. An array stores items in one contiguous block of memory, divided into slots of equal size. That layout is what makes indexing cheap. To find item i, the machine takes the address where the block starts, adds i times the slot width, and reads that location. It is one multiplication and one addition, whatever the index, so reaching item five thousand costs the same as reaching item zero. No walking is needed. The board's memory card is a model of that idea. A Python list is built on the same principle, with one twist. Its slots hold references to objects, not the objects themselves, so the parcel records live elsewhere in memory and the list's block just points at them. The exact layout is an implementation detail of CPython. What we rely on is that indexing a list is a constant-time operation. Indexing makes a useful technique possible, called prefix sums. Suppose the planner records the grams dispatched in each hour of a shift. In one pass we build a second list, where entry i holds the total of the first i hours. After that, the total for any range of hours is one subtraction: prefix at j minus prefix at i. The output checks it against a direct sum for hours two to four. Both give seven thousand five hundred. So a linear amount of preparation buys constant time for every later query. A related idea is the rolling total over a fixed window, here three hours. Instead of re-adding three numbers at each step, it adds the hour that enters the window and subtracts the hour that leaves. Both techniques assume the data does not change. If one hour's figure is corrected, every later prefix entry must be rebuilt, which costs linear time. The final chapter returns to structures that handle updates.

An array's block has a fixed size, chosen when it is allocated. Yet a Python list lets you append forever. The structure that reconciles the two is the dynamic array. It keeps a block with some spare capacity. While there is room, an append writes into the next free slot, which is constant time. When the block is full, it allocates a new block twice as large, copies every existing item across, and then appends. That copy costs time proportional to the number of items, so a single append can be expensive. The question is what this costs over many appends. The script on the board is a teaching model of exactly this strategy, and it counts every element copied by a resize. Resizes happen when the size reaches one, two, four, eight, and so on, copying that many items each time. So over n appends the total copying is a geometric sum, one plus two plus four, up to the largest power below n, and that sum is less than two n. Spread across n appends, that is fewer than two copies per append, whatever n is. The output confirms it: one point four copies per append at five items, and about one at a million. This style of argument is called amortised analysis. It says that the total cost of any sequence of n appends is at most a constant times n, so each append costs constant time on average over the sequence. Amortised cost is not expected cost. There is no randomness and no assumed distribution. It is a guarantee for every sequence, even though one particular append, the one that triggers a resize, is slow. One honest caveat. The class here is a model. CPython grows lists by a smaller factor than two, with some extra headroom, but the argument is the same: any constant growth factor above one gives constant amortised time.

A linked list stores a sequence differently. Instead of one block, each item lives in its own node, and each node holds a reference to the next node. The list is reached through a single reference to the first node, called the head, and the last node points at None. The key to reasoning about linked lists is to keep two costs apart. Locating a node means walking from the head, following next references one at a time, so finding a parcel by identifier costs linear time. Changing the list at a node you already hold is different. It only rewrites a few references, so it costs constant time, whatever the length. The board shows both. First we walk to P two-twenty-one. Then we insert P three-seventeen after it, with two writes. The new node's next is set to P four-fifty-eight, and then P two-twenty-one's next is set to the new node. The order of those writes matters. If P two-twenty-one were redirected first, the only reference to the rest of the list would be overwritten, and everything after it would be lost. Deletion after a node is a single write: the previous node's next skips over the deleted one. The output shows the list before and after insertion, after deleting the new node again, and after deleting the head. Deleting the head is a boundary case, because there is no previous node. The head reference itself has to move. Empty lists and single-node lists need their own traces too, since the loops that walk the list run zero or one times there. The cost of all this flexibility is indexing. There is no address arithmetic, so reaching position i means walking i links. A linked list is the right choice when you already hold references to the places you change, and the wrong one when you mainly look things up by position.

A doubly linked list gives each node a second reference, to the previous node. With links in both directions, a node can be removed when you hold only that node, without searching for its predecessor. The extra references also bring extra ways to get things wrong, and two ideas keep them under control. The first is a sentinel. Instead of letting the list end in None at each side, we add one dummy node that holds no data and closes the list into a ring. The sentinel's next is the first real node, and its prev is the last. An empty list is just the sentinel pointing at itself. With a sentinel, every real node always has a real previous and a real next node, so insertion and removal never need special cases for the front, the back, or an empty list. The code on the board has no checks for None at all. The second idea is a structural invariant. For every node, following next and then prev must lead back to the same node. Insertion before a node rewrites four links: the new node's prev and next, and the two neighbours that now point at it. Removal rewrites two. Each operation is constant time, and each must leave the invariant true. The pids method checks the invariant with an assertion on every node it visits, so a broken link fails loudly rather than producing a quietly wrong list. The output shows the empty list, three insertions including one in the middle, and two removals, each made with nothing but the node itself. The trade-off is memory and care. Each node carries two references instead of one, and each operation has more writes to order correctly. In return, removal given a node and operations at both ends are all constant time.

A stack is a sequence that allows only two changes: push an item on top, and pop the item from the top. The most recently added item is always the first to leave, which is why stacks are called last in, first out. In Python, a list makes a good stack, as long as both operations happen at the end. Append and pop with no argument are both constant time. Stacks fit any problem where the most recently opened thing must be closed first. The classic example is checking that brackets are balanced, as in a template for parcel labels or a piece of code. The checker on the board reads the text one character at a time. Each opening bracket is pushed, together with its position. Each closing bracket must match the opener on top of the stack, and if it does, that opener is popped. The memory card shows the stack after reading the first three characters of the first test: the parenthesis on top, opened last, is the first that must close. The output shows the possible outcomes. Properly nested text is balanced. In the second test, a closing parenthesis arrives while a square bracket is still on top, so the checker reports a mismatch at position two. In the third, the text ends with an opener still on the stack, which means it was never closed. The empty string is balanced, and ordinary letters are simply skipped. Stacks appear throughout computing. Undo history is a stack of previous states. Parsers use stacks to handle nested expressions. And the call stack from the last chapter is exactly this structure: each function call pushes a frame, and each return pops one. That is why every recursive algorithm can be rewritten as a loop with an explicit stack, a technique chapter eight uses to escape Python's recursion limit.

A queue is the opposite discipline to a stack. Items join at the back and leave from the front, so the first to arrive is the first served, like parcels waiting at a loading bay. There is a common trap when building a queue from a Python list. Appending at the back is cheap, but removing from the front with pop zero shifts every remaining item one place to the left. That is linear time for each removal, so a queue that handles n parcels does quadratic work overall. A ring buffer avoids the shifting entirely. It uses a fixed array, an index called head that marks the front, and a count of how many items are stored. The next free slot at the back is head plus size, taken modulo the capacity. Dequeuing reads the item at head and moves head forward by one, also modulo the capacity. Nothing ever moves, and both operations are constant time. The modulo is what makes the array behave like a circle. The board shows the state after five arrivals and two departures in a buffer of capacity four. The head has advanced to slot two, and the newest parcel, P five-twelve, has wrapped round into slot zero. Reading from head onwards, round the circle, gives the queue in order. A fixed capacity raises a question every queue design must answer: what happens when it is full? The buffer can refuse new items, overwrite the oldest, make the producer wait, or grow into a larger array. This one refuses, by raising an overflow error, as the last line of output shows. None of these choices is universally right. A sensor log might prefer overwriting, while a parcel queue must never silently drop a parcel. Whatever the choice, it belongs in the contract, alongside the operations themselves.

A deque, short for double-ended queue, generalises both stacks and queues. It allows items to be added and removed at both ends. Python provides one in the collections module, and its four end operations, append, append left, pop and pop left, all run in constant time. So a single structure can serve as a stack, using one end, or as a queue, adding at one end and removing at the other. For any queue in Python, a deque is the standard replacement for popping from the front of a list. The script on the board uses a deque as the loading order at a depot. Ordinary parcels join at the back with append. An urgent parcel jumps the queue with append left, so it is served next. The output shows the urgent parcel at the front, and then one parcel leaving from each end. Deques have a second useful feature, a maximum length. When a deque created with max len is full, appending at one end silently drops an item from the opposite end. That makes a bounded history very easy to keep. Here the deque holds only the last three scanned parcels. After four scans, the oldest has fallen off the front, as the output shows. Remember the earlier point about capacity management: this is the overwrite policy, chosen deliberately. It is also worth knowing what a deque is not. It is not an array. CPython builds it from linked blocks of items, so indexing near either end is fast, but indexing near the middle takes time proportional to the distance. If a program mostly reads items by position, a list is the better choice. Finally, rotate moves items from one end to the other. Rotating by one, at the end of the script, takes the last item and puts it at the front. Rotating by k costs time proportional to k, since each step is one move between the ends.

This chapter has built several representations of a sequence, and none of them is best at everything. The table on the board compares them operation by operation. A Python list indexes in constant time and appends at the back in amortised constant time, but inserting or removing at the front shifts everything. A linked list changes the list in constant time at a node you already hold, but has to walk to find anything. A deque is constant time at both ends and slow in the middle. A ring buffer is constant time at both ends and by index, but has a fixed capacity. So the choice should follow the workload. Count which operations the program performs most often, and choose the structure that makes those cheap. If dispatch mostly looks parcels up by position, use a list. If it mostly adds and removes at the ends, use a deque. If it splices routes at known points, a linked list earns its keep. One factor does not appear in the table at all. Array items sit next to each other in memory, so scanning an array reads memory in order, which modern processors do very quickly. Linked nodes can be scattered anywhere, so walking them is slower than the same number of steps over an array. The cost model treats every step as equal. Timings, as the last chapter showed, do not. Each node is also a separate object with its own overhead, so a linked list uses more memory per item than an array. Mutation adds one more hazard, and it is a classic. Multiplying a list repeats its references, not its contents. So writing a list containing a row of zeros, times three, creates three references to one single row. The script sets one cell and every row changes, because there is only one row, and the is test confirms it. Building the rows with a comprehension creates three separate lists, and the same assignment then changes only one cell. It is the aliasing lesson from chapter one, now inside a data structure.

This chapter is about order: how to sort data, and how sorted data makes searching cheap. It starts with a question that is easy to skip. What exactly does sorted mean? A sort needs an order, and an order has three parts: a key that says what to compare, a direction, and a rule for what happens when two keys are equal. In Python the key is a function. Sorting parcels with a key that returns the weight orders them by weight. A tuple key orders by its first component, and breaks ties with the next, so a key of depot and weight sorts by depot, and by weight within each depot. Whatever the key, the comparisons must be consistent. If a is less than b, b must not also be less than a, or no sorted order exists. Equal keys are called ties, and duplicates are common in real data. In the script, three parcels weigh eight hundred grams. A sort is stable if tied items keep the order they had in the input. The table on the board shows those three parcels: P two-twenty-one, P five-twelve and P six hundred, still in their input order after sorting by weight. Python's built-in sorted function and the list sort method are guaranteed to be stable, by the language documentation. Stability is more than tidiness, because it composes. Sort by weight, and then sort the result stably by depot. Within each depot, the parcels stay in weight order, because the second sort never reorders ties. The result is the same as one sort by the tuple key, and the script checks that equality: true. This two-pass technique is how multi-key sorts are done when the keys have different directions, or come from different sources. It also explains why the later radix sort works. Not every sorting algorithm is stable, and the next sections show one that is not.

Sorting pays for itself through searching. On sorted data, a single comparison with the middle item tells us which half the target must be in, so the other half can be discarded. Repeating that halving finds the answer in about log n comparisons. Binary search is famous for off-by-one errors, and the cure is to write down an interval invariant, as the code on the board does. Everything before lo is less than the target. Everything from hi onwards is greater than or equal to the target. Between them is a region still unknown. Each step looks at the middle of that region. If the middle item is less than the target, lo moves just past it. Otherwise hi moves down to it. Either way the invariant still holds and the unknown region shrinks. When lo equals hi, the unknown region is empty, and the invariant says exactly what lo is: the first index whose item is at least the target. The memory card shows that final state for a target of twenty-five hundred: lo and hi meet at index four. With duplicates, there are two useful boundaries. The first position of a key, which Python's bisect left returns, and the position just after the last one, which bisect right returns. The output shows both agreeing with the hand-written version. Their difference counts the copies: three parcels of eight hundred grams. A missing key is not an error. Bisect returns the position where it would go, so a thousand would go at index three. One cost is worth separating. Finding the right slot in a sorted list is logarithmic. But inserting there, with insort, still shifts every later item, which is linear. A sorted list is excellent for lookups and slow for frequent insertions, which is the motivation for the search trees of chapter six.

Before the fast algorithms, two simple ones, which serve as baselines and teach two different invariants. Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix. Its invariant is that the first i items are sorted among themselves. To extend it, it takes the next item and shifts every larger item in the prefix one place right, until the gap is where the new item belongs. Selection sort uses a stronger invariant. The first i positions hold the i smallest items overall, already in their final places. To extend it, it scans the rest of the list for the minimum and swaps it into position i. Both are quadratic in the worst case, but the instrumented script shows how differently they behave. On a hundred items that are already sorted, insertion sort shifts nothing at all, because every item is already in place. On reversed input it shifts four thousand nine hundred and fifty times, which is n times n minus one over two. Its cost depends on how far the input is from sorted, which is why it is called adaptive, and why it is fast on nearly sorted data. Selection sort makes exactly four thousand nine hundred and fifty comparisons on both inputs. It cannot notice that work is already done. It does have one strength: it makes at most n minus one swaps, which matters when writing an item is far more expensive than comparing it. Insertion sort is stable, since an item never moves past an equal one. Selection sort is not, and the last line shows why. Sorting pairs by their number alone, the swap that brings the one to the front sends two a to the back, past its equal two b. The tie's input order is lost. A long-distance swap is the usual way stability breaks, and it returns in quicksort.

Merge sort is the first algorithm in this course built by divide and conquer. The idea has three steps: divide the problem into smaller parts, solve each part recursively, and combine the answers. For sorting, divide means split the list in half, and conquer means sort each half by the same method. All the real work is in combining, an operation called merge. Merge takes two sorted lists and builds one sorted list by repeatedly comparing their front items and taking the smaller. When the fronts are equal, it takes from the left half first, and that single choice, less than or equal rather than less than, is what makes merge sort stable. The script prints every merge, indented by recursion depth. Single items merge into pairs, pairs into fours, and the two fours into the final eight. Notice the two eights: the one that started on the left stays first. The running time follows from the recursion tree of chapter two. The recurrence is T of n equals two T of n over two, plus linear work for the merge. At every level of the tree, the merges together handle all n items, so each level costs linear time. There are log two of n levels, three for eight items, so the total is n log n. And unlike the simple sorts, that bound is the same for every input. There is no bad case. The price is space. Merging needs somewhere to put its output, so merge sort uses linear extra memory, and this teaching version also copies with slices. It is worth knowing what Python itself uses. The built-in sort is also merge-based. It finds runs that are already in order and merges them carefully, which makes it adaptive and stable. It is not the simple version on the board, and it is certainly not quicksort.

Quicksort is also divide and conquer, but it puts the work in the opposite place. Merge sort splits trivially and works hard to combine. Quicksort works hard to split, and then needs no combining at all. The splitting step is called partition. Choose one item as the pivot, then rearrange the subarray so that items less than or equal to the pivot come first and larger items come after. The memory card shows the invariant the partition loop maintains. From lo up to i, everything is at most the pivot. From i up to j, everything is greater. From j onwards, nothing has been looked at yet. Each step examines the next unseen item and, if it is small, swaps it into the first region. At the end the pivot is swapped into position i, which is its final place in the sorted output. Then each side is sorted recursively. Everything about quicksort's cost depends on the pivot. If each partition splits the items roughly in half, there are about log n levels and the total is n log n. If the pivot is always the largest or smallest item, one side is empty, there are n levels, and the cost is quadratic. The output shows exactly this. Using the last item as the pivot on input that is already sorted gives the worst possible splits: four hundred and ninety-nine thousand, five hundred comparisons for a thousand items. A random pivot on the same input needs ten thousand five hundred and seventy-six. With random pivots, the expected cost is n log n on every input, because the randomness belongs to the algorithm, the point made in chapter two. Two practical details. Recursing on the smaller side and looping on the larger keeps the stack depth logarithmic even in bad cases. And partition swaps items over long distances, so quicksort is not stable.

Every sort so far has worked by comparing items. When the keys have extra structure, we can do better than comparing. The simplest case is keys that are small integers, say from zero up to k minus one. Counting sort makes one pass to count how many items have each key. From the counts it works out where each key's block of output must start: key zero starts at zero, key one starts after all the zeros, and so on. A final pass places each item in its key's next free slot. Because that last pass reads the input in its original order, items with equal keys stay in order, so counting sort is stable. The total cost is n plus k. That is excellent when k is small, and terrible when k is huge, since a key range of a billion needs a billion counters. Radix sort extends the idea to larger keys by splitting them into digits. It sorts by the last digit first, then by the next digit, and so on, using a stable sort for each pass. The output shows three passes over seven parcel numbers. After the first pass they are ordered by their last digit. After the second, by their last two digits. After the third, completely. Stability is what makes this work. When two numbers share a tens digit, the second pass keeps them in the order the first pass gave them, which is the correct order by their units digit. Each pass costs n plus ten, so three-digit numbers take three linear passes. These algorithms rest on an assumption that must be stated: the keys are integers in a known, small range, or can be split into such digits. Under that assumption they are not comparison sorts at all, which is why the lower bound in the next section does not apply to them.

Sometimes we need one particular rank, not the whole sorted order. The median weight, the tenth heaviest parcel, the ninety-fifth percentile of delivery times. The item that would sit at position k in sorted order is called the k-th order statistic. Sorting and indexing finds it in n log n time, but that does more work than needed. Quickselect borrows quicksort's partition. Choose a random pivot and split the items into those smaller than the pivot, those equal to it, and those larger. Now compare k with the sizes of the groups. If k falls among the smaller items, the answer is in that group. If it falls in the equal group, the pivot itself is the answer. Otherwise, it is in the larger group, at a shifted rank. Unlike quicksort, only one side needs further work. The script finds the median of ten thousand and one random weights and checks it against sorting: both give four thousand five hundred and ninety-six. The expected cost is linear, and the argument is the geometric sum again. A random pivot falls in the middle half of the values with probability one half, and then the side we keep has at most three quarters of the items. So on average each round shrinks the problem by a constant fraction, and the total work is n plus three quarters of n plus nine sixteenths of n, and so on, which is at most four n. This seeded run scanned about three and a half n elements. As with quicksort, unlucky pivots can make it quadratic in the worst case, although that is extremely improbable with random choices. If a worst-case guarantee is required, a method called median of medians chooses the pivot deterministically and achieves linear time in the worst case, at the price of much larger constant factors.

We now have sorting algorithms that take n log n time. Could a cleverer one do better? For comparison sorts, the answer is no, and the argument is one of the most elegant in the subject. Any algorithm that learns about the input only by comparing pairs of items can be drawn as a decision tree. Each internal node is a comparison with two outcomes, and each leaf is a final answer, one particular ordering of the input. The board shows the tree for three items, a, b and c. Since any of the n factorial orderings could be the right answer, the tree needs at least n factorial leaves. A binary tree of depth d has at most two to the d leaves, so the depth, the number of comparisons on the worst path, must be at least log two of n factorial. For three items that is three comparisons. The table shows how log of n factorial grows: it is Theta of n log n. So no comparison sort can beat n log n in the worst case, and merge sort is optimal among them. The bound assumes the comparison model. Counting and radix sorts escape it by using the structure of integer keys, which is no contradiction. Sorted order is useful beyond sorting. The two pointers technique finds two parcels whose weights add up to a capacity. Start one pointer at the lightest and one at the heaviest. If the pair is too light, move the low pointer up. If too heavy, move the high pointer down. On sorted weights each move safely discards one item, and the pair is found. On unsorted weights the same moves discard the wrong items, and the output shows it returning None, although a pair exists. Choosing a strategy follows from all this. For a few lookups, a linear scan is fine. For many, sort once and binary search. For small integer keys, use counting or radix sort, and for one rank, quickselect.

Chapter one's lookup scanned the list. Sorting made lookups logarithmic. This chapter goes further, to lookups that cost constant time on average, and it starts with what the structure promises. A map stores one value for each key: parcel identifier to depot, for instance. A set stores keys alone, and answers only whether a key is present. The operations are put, get, delete and membership, and notice what is missing. Order is not part of the contract. Keys are found by equality, not by position, and the goal is expected constant time per operation, with no sorting at all. Python's dict and set provide exactly this. The script on the board shows the contract and three ways it can surprise. First, a key must be hashable. It needs a hash function consistent with its equality: any two equal keys must have the same hash. Lists can change, so Python refuses them as keys with a type error. Second, keys are compared by equality, and equality can cross types. In Python, one, one point nought and True are all equal, and they have equal hashes, so a dict built from all three ends up with a single entry. It keeps the first key that was inserted and the last value that was assigned. Third, key lifetime. The Tag class computes its hash from a field that can be changed. The script stores a tag in a set, then changes its identifier. Now the stored object sits in the bucket for its old hash, while lookups for it go to the bucket for its new one. The output shows that neither the old value nor the new value finds it. The object is still in the set, but unreachable. The rule is simple: never change a key while it is stored in a hash-based structure, which is why Python's built-in immutable types make the safest keys.

A hash table turns lookup into indexing. To see the idea, start with the simplest case, direct addressing. If parcel numbers were small integers, the number could be the index: store parcel one hundred and four in slot one hundred and four. Every operation would be a single array access. The trouble is space. Direct addressing needs one slot for every possible key, whether it is used or not. Ten-digit identifiers would need ten billion slots to store a few thousand parcels. A hash table keeps the speed and drops the waste in two steps. First, a hash function turns any key into an integer. Then the integer is reduced modulo m, the number of buckets, to pick an index between zero and m minus one. The script uses a simple polynomial hash on the characters of the identifier, which is deterministic, so its output can be checked. Python's own hash for strings is randomised each time the interpreter starts, for a reason the sixth section explains. A good hash function spreads similar keys far apart and depends on every character of the key, so that P three-seventeen and P three-eighteen land in unrelated buckets. Even so, look at the output. With eight buckets, six identifiers already produce two collisions, pairs of keys that share a bucket. This is not bad luck. There are vastly more possible keys than buckets, so some keys must share. Collisions are certain, and a hash table is defined by how it handles them. The next two sections show the two main strategies. One last clarification, because the word is overloaded. The hash functions used for tables are designed to be fast, not secret. They provide no security, and they are not encryption. Cryptographic hashes are a different tool, built for a different contract.

The first strategy for collisions is separate chaining. Each bucket holds a small list, called a chain, of every key and value pair that hashed to that bucket. To put a pair, hash the key to find its bucket, then scan that bucket's chain. If the key is already there, overwrite its value. Otherwise append a new pair. To get, hash to the bucket and scan its chain, comparing keys with equality. If the scan reaches the end, the key is absent and the answer is None. Notice the two different roles. The hash only chooses where to look. Equality decides whether a stored key is actually the one we want. That is why the two must agree, the rule from the first section. The board shows a table with four buckets after six insertions. Three identifiers hashed to bucket zero, so its chain has three pairs. Bucket three is empty. A lookup for P four-fifty-eight checks one pair, while a lookup in bucket zero may check three. So the cost depends on chain length. If n keys are spread evenly over m buckets, the average chain has n over m pairs. That ratio is called the load factor. An operation costs one step to hash plus the length of the chain it scans, constant plus n over m. As long as the load factor stays bounded by a constant, every operation is constant time on average. Keeping it bounded is the subject of section five. Chaining is simple and robust. Deletion is easy, since a pair is simply removed from one chain, and the table keeps working even when it is overloaded, just more slowly. Its costs are memory and locality. Every chain is a separate list object, and following chains jumps around memory, which open addressing, next, avoids.

The second strategy, open addressing, keeps every key in the array itself, with no chains. When a key's slot is taken, it moves on to another slot according to a fixed rule called a probe sequence. The simplest rule is linear probing: try the hash slot, then the next one, then the next, wrapping round at the end of the array. A lookup follows exactly the same probe path. It stops with success when it finds the key, and stops with failure when it reaches an empty slot, because an insertion would have used that empty slot if the key had been added. The board shows eight slots after five insertions. P three-seventeen hashed to slot four, found P two-twenty-one already there, and was stored one step along, in slot five. Now consider deleting P two-twenty-one. The obvious approach is to empty its slot. But that breaks the reasoning behind every lookup. A search for P three-seventeen starts at slot four, finds it empty, and stops, concluding that the key is absent. The output confirms it: the naive deletion returns None, even though P three-seventeen is still sitting in slot five. It has become unreachable. The standard fix is a tombstone. Instead of emptying the slot, mark it as deleted. Lookups treat a tombstone as occupied by something else and keep probing, so the path to slot five stays intact. The output shows the tombstone version finding P three-seventeen in slot five. Insertions may reuse tombstone slots. Tombstones have a cost of their own. They lengthen probe paths without holding any data, so a table with many deletions gets slower, and is eventually rebuilt from scratch to clear them. In return, open addressing stores everything in one array, which is compact and fast to scan.

Both strategies depend on one number, the load factor: the number of keys n divided by the number of slots m. With chaining it is the average chain length. With open addressing it measures how full the array is, and probe paths grow very quickly as the array fills. Linear probing in particular degrades sharply as the load factor approaches one, so tables keep it well below that. The set on the board doubles its array whenever an insertion would push the load factor above one half. The plot shows the resulting sawtooth. The load factor climbs towards the threshold as keys arrive, then halves at each resize. A resize is called rehashing, and it is more than copying. Every key's bucket is its hash modulo m, and m has just changed, so every key must be placed again in the new array. One resize therefore costs time proportional to the number of keys. The output counts the moves: one thousand insertions caused one thousand and twenty moves in total. That is the dynamic array argument from chapter three again. Because the array doubles, resizes happen at sizes four, eight, sixteen and so on, and the total work is a geometric sum, linear in the number of insertions. So each insertion is amortised constant time, even though the occasional insertion that triggers a resize is slow. This is why hash table costs are stated over sequences of operations rather than single ones. Most operations are cheap, a few are expensive, and the total is linear. One more design point: a table that also shrinks when keys are deleted needs a lower threshold well below the upper one. Otherwise a sequence of alternating inserts and deletes at the boundary could trigger a resize on every operation, a failure called thrashing.

It is common to hear that hash tables are constant time. That is an expected cost, and it rests on an assumption worth stating precisely. The assumption is that keys spread evenly over the buckets, as if each were placed at random. Under that assumption, the expected chain length is the load factor, n over m, and with the load factor bounded, every operation is constant time on average. But the worst case is very different. If every key lands in the same bucket, the table degenerates into one long list, and every operation costs linear time. The question is whether inputs can push a table into that worst case, and the answer is that an adversary can. The script uses a deliberately weak hash, the sum of the character codes. Any rearrangement of the same characters has the same sum, so all twenty-four anagrams of P one-two-three-four land in one bucket. The output shows the average lookup scanning twenty-four entries, compared with about two point four for twenty-four ordinary keys. That is a tenfold slowdown from twenty-four keys. An attacker who can choose the keys sent to a server, for instance the field names in a web request, can force every insertion into one chain, turning a linear amount of work into quadratic work. Attacks of this kind have taken real services offline. There are several defences. First, hash functions that mix every bit and position of the key, so simple rearrangements do not collide. Second, a random seed chosen when the program starts, so an attacker cannot predict which keys collide. This is why Python randomises the hash of strings in each process, and why the earlier examples used their own deterministic hash. Third, some libraries bound the damage by storing large buckets as balanced trees, which caps the worst case at logarithmic time.

Most practical uses of hashing come down to one idea: remember what you have already seen, and look it up in constant time. Three patterns cover a great deal of everyday code. The first is a frequency table. Counting how many times each parcel was scanned takes one pass with a counter, a dict from item to count, so the whole job is linear. The output shows P one-oh-four scanned three times and P two-twenty-one twice. The second is deduplication. Building a dict from the scans, with dict from keys, keeps the first occurrence of each parcel and discards the rest, in a single pass. The third is memo lookup: store each computed answer under its input, so a repeated question is answered from the table instead of being recomputed. Chapter twelve builds dynamic programming on exactly this. The script ends with a sliding window, the bounded technique from the plan. The question is the longest run of consecutive scans with no parcel repeated. A dict called last remembers the most recent position of each parcel. The window is from start to end. When the next scan repeats a parcel whose last position is inside the window, start jumps just past that earlier copy, which restores the condition. Both start and end only ever move forward, so the whole scan is linear. Here the longest run has five scans. It is worth being precise about what Python's dict promises. It keeps keys in insertion order, which is reliable and documented, but insertion order is not sorted order. A dict cannot efficiently answer the smallest key, the next key after this one, or every key in a range. When a problem needs order as well as fast lookup, a hash table is the wrong tool, and the ordered trees of the next chapter are the right one.

Lists arrange items in a line. Trees arrange them in a hierarchy, and that shape is what lets ordered data be both searched and changed quickly. A tree has one node at the top, called the root. Every other node has exactly one parent, the node directly above it, and the nodes directly below a node are its children. A node with no children is a leaf, and a node with at least one child is internal. The board shows the tree this chapter keeps returning to, an index of depot numbers with three hundred and seventeen at the root. Two measurements matter. The depth of a node is the number of edges on the path from the root down to it, so the root has depth zero. The height of the tree is the greatest depth of any node, two here. In a binary tree, each node has at most two children, a left child and a right child, and binary trees are this chapter's focus. A tree can be stored in several ways. The examples use linked nodes, each holding a key and references to its left and right children, much like the linked lists of chapter three. When a tree is complete, filled level by level, it can be stored in a plain array with no references at all, which is exactly how the heap of the next chapter works. And when nodes can have many children, each node can keep a list of them. Trees are naturally recursive. A tree is either empty, or a root with a left subtree and a right subtree, which are trees themselves. So measurements are defined recursively too. The height of an empty tree is minus one. Otherwise it is one plus the height of the taller child. The script computes size, height and leaves this way. Height is the number to watch, because every operation in this chapter follows one path from the root, and costs time proportional to the height.

A traversal visits every node of a tree exactly once, and the interesting question is the order. The three depth-first orders differ only in when a node is visited relative to its subtrees. Pre-order visits the node first, then its left subtree, then its right, which is the natural order for copying a tree from the top down. Post-order visits both subtrees first and the node last, which suits freeing a tree or computing totals from the children upwards. In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. For a binary search tree that order produces the keys in sorted order, as the output shows. The recursive version is short, and its base case is explicit: an empty subtree returns immediately. Every recursive call is on a smaller tree, so the recursion ends. Correctness follows by induction on the size of the tree. If the traversal is correct on both subtrees, then visiting the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree visits every key in this tree in sorted order. The base case, the empty tree, is trivially correct. The same traversal can be written without recursion, using an explicit stack. Starting at the root, push nodes while moving left. When there is no further left child, pop a node, visit it, and move to its right child. The memory card shows the stack just before fifty is visited: fifty on top, then one hundred and four, then the root. Those are exactly the calls the recursive version would have waiting, which is the point. The call stack from chapter two is a stack like any other. The iterative version matters for deep trees. Both versions need stack space proportional to the height, but the explicit stack has no recursion limit, so it survives the badly shaped trees of section five.

A binary search tree combines the tree shape with the ordering idea from chapter four. It maintains one rule at every node, the binary search tree property. Every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key, and every key in its right subtree is larger. That single rule makes search very direct. At each node, one comparison tells us whether the target is here, in the left subtree, or in the right subtree, and the other subtree can be ignored entirely. So a search follows a single path from the root downwards, much like binary search on a sorted list. The demo prints those paths. Looking for two-twenty-one, the search starts at three hundred and seventeen and goes left, reaches one hundred and four and goes right, and finds two-twenty-one: three nodes. Looking for three hundred, it follows three-seventeen, one hundred and four and two-twenty-one, then tries to step into an empty right subtree. That proves three hundred is absent, because the property says it could not be anywhere else. A search costs comparisons proportional to the length of the path, which is at most the height of the tree. Insertion reuses the search. Search for the new key, and when the search falls off the tree, attach a new leaf at exactly that spot. The demo inserts three hundred and searches again: the new node sits right where the failed search ended. Every comparison made on the way down agreed with the property, so the property still holds. The code also states a duplicate-key policy, as chapter one insisted. Inserting a key that already exists overwrites its value, so the tree holds one entry per key, like a dict. Other policies are possible, such as keeping a count or a list of values per key, and the choice belongs in the contract.

Deletion is the operation where binary search trees need the most care, because removing a node must not break the ordering of everything around it. There are three cases, and the code handles each one explicitly. The first case is a leaf, a node with no children. Deleting fifty simply replaces it with an empty subtree. The second case is a node with one child. Four hundred has a single right child, four hundred and twenty. Deleting it lets that child take its place. Every key in the child's subtree was already on the correct side of four hundred's parent, so the property still holds. Both cases come down to changing one reference, once the node has been found. The third case is a node with two children, and it needs an idea. Three hundred and seventeen, the root, has both. Removing it would leave two subtrees needing a single parent. Instead, find its successor: the next larger key, which is the smallest key in its right subtree. Here that is four hundred and twenty. The successor is larger than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right, so it can take the deleted key's place without breaking the property. Copy four hundred and twenty into the root's position, then delete the original four hundred and twenty from the right subtree. That second deletion is always one of the easy cases, because the smallest key in a subtree has no left child. The output checks the result in the simplest way possible: after every deletion, the in-order traversal is still sorted, and after the third, the root's key has become four hundred and twenty. Each deletion follows at most two paths down the tree, one to the node and one to its successor, so the cost is again proportional to the height.

Every binary search tree operation so far costs time proportional to the height of the tree. Nothing so far keeps the height small, and the shape of the tree depends entirely on the order in which keys arrive. Consider inserting the keys one, two, three and four in sorted order. Each new key is larger than everything already present, so it always goes right. The tree becomes a chain, drawn on the board, with height n minus one. It is a linked list with extra steps, and search in it is linear. Beside it, the same four keys inserted in the order three, one, four, two make a bushier tree of height two. The script measures this at a thousand keys. Inserted in sorted order, the tree has height nine hundred and ninety-nine. Inserted in a shuffled order, the same keys give a tree of height twenty-one. And the best possible height for a thousand keys is nine, about log base two of n. Random insertion orders produce trees of logarithmic height on average, which is a reassuring result. But an average over random orders is not a guarantee, and real data is rarely in random order. Parcel identifiers are often issued in sequence, and dates and timestamps arrive sorted by nature. So the bad case is not an exotic adversary. It is ordinary data. The skewed tree also strains recursion. The recursive height function on a chain of a thousand nodes needs a thousand stack frames, more than Python's default limit, which is why the script raises the limit, and why the iterative traversals of section two matter. To guarantee logarithmic height whatever the insertion order, the tree has to repair its own shape as it changes. That is called rebalancing, and the next section shows the classic way to do it.

An AVL tree is a binary search tree that repairs its own shape. It keeps one extra invariant: at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most one. To check that cheaply, each node stores its own height, and a small function called fix recomputes it from the children's heights. After an insertion, the recursion returns back up the path to the root, fixing heights and computing the balance at each node, the left height minus the right height. If a balance reaches two or minus two, the node is repaired with a rotation. A rotation lifts a child above its parent. The board shows the simplest case. Inserting fifty, one hundred and four and two-twenty-one in order builds a chain leaning right, and the balance at fifty is minus two. A left rotation at fifty makes one hundred and four the root, with fifty as its left child and two-twenty-one as its right. Only a few references change, so a rotation is constant time. Crucially, it preserves the in-order sequence. Fifty, one hundred and four, two-twenty-one, before and after, so the search tree property survives. The code distinguishes four cases. When the imbalance is on the outside, left-left or right-right, one rotation fixes it. When it bends inwards, left-right or right-left, a first rotation straightens the bend and a second one fixes it. That is a double rotation. The output shows the guarantee in action. Seven keys inserted in sorted order, the worst order for a plain binary search tree, produce a perfectly balanced tree of height two. In general, an AVL tree's height is at most about one point four four times log base two of n, so every operation is logarithmic in the worst case. Red-black trees, used in many libraries, enforce a looser balance in exchange for fewer rotations on update.

A balanced search tree answers lookups in logarithmic time. With a small addition, it can answer much richer questions just as fast. The technique is called augmentation: store some extra information at each node, chosen so that it can be computed from the node and its children alone. The classic example is subtree size. Each node records how many nodes its subtree contains, which is one plus the sizes of its two children. The board shows the depot tree with those sizes, seven at the root and one at each leaf. Because a size depends only on the children, every insertion, deletion or rotation can update it in constant time per node along the path it already walks, so maintaining it costs nothing extra asymptotically. Sizes make rank queries possible. The rank of a key is how many stored keys are smaller. Walk down from the root as in a search. Whenever the walk goes right, every key in the left subtree, and the node itself, are smaller than the target, so add the left subtree's size plus one in a single step, without visiting those nodes. The output shows four keys smaller than four hundred: fifty, one hundred and four, two-twenty-one and three-seventeen. A range count follows directly. The number of keys between one hundred and four hundred and fifty is the rank just past the top of the range, minus the rank of the bottom, which is four. Both cost time proportional to the height. Any value that can be computed from a node and its children can be stored this way, such as the total weight of the parcels in a subtree, or the smallest deadline. It is worth contrasting with Python's dict. A dict keeps insertion order and answers exact lookups, but it is not an ordered search tree, and it has no efficient way to answer rank or range questions at all.

Everything so far has assumed that data lives in memory, where following a reference costs about the same as a comparison. When the data lives on disk or another slow store, that assumption fails, and the cost model has to change. Reading one block from storage takes far longer than thousands of comparisons on data already in memory. So for data on disk, the honest measure of cost is the number of blocks transferred, and comparisons inside a block are nearly free by comparison. Under that model, a binary tree is a poor choice. Each node holds one key, so every level of the tree means another block read, and a billion keys need about thirty levels. A B-tree is designed for this model. Each node holds many keys in sorted order and has one more child than it has keys, and a node is sized to fill one block. The board shows a small example.
