The root holds three-seventeen and six hundred, and its three children hold the keys below, between and above them. A search reads one node, scans its keys to choose a child, and reads one child block per level. B-trees keep all their leaves at the same depth, and when a node overflows it splits in two, so every node stays at least half full. Wide nodes make the tree very shallow. The output computes the number of levels for a billion keys. With two-way branching it is thirty block reads per lookup. With two hundred and fifty-six way branching, it is four. This is why databases and file systems index their data with B-trees and their variants. The lesson reaches beyond trees. The best data structure depends on what the cost model counts. Change what is expensive, and the right answer changes with it, which is a theme the final chapter returns to.

The delivery planner often needs only one thing from its pending parcels: the most urgent one, right now, while new parcels keep arriving. Sorting everything would answer that, but it does far more work than needed, and it would have to be redone after every arrival. A priority queue is the structure built for exactly this job. Its contract has three operations. Push adds an item with a priority. Pop removes and returns the most urgent item. Peek returns it without removing it. Notice what the contract does not promise: anything about the order of the remaining items. That freedom is what makes it cheaper than a sorted list. Python provides a priority queue through the heapq module, which keeps a list in heap order, and it has one subtlety worth seeing early. Heapq compares whole entries. If two entries are tuples with equal priorities, Python goes on to compare the next element of each tuple, here the parcels themselves. Parcel records define no ordering, so the script fails with a type error the moment two priorities tie. The standard fix is to make each entry a triple: the priority, then a sequence number that increases with every push, then the item. The sequence number breaks every tie, so the items are never compared. It also gives equal priorities a well-defined order: first in, first out, as the output shows. Two parcels of urgency one come out in the order they were pushed. Requirements like these shape the design and should be settled up front. Can a priority change after the item is queued? Is the order among equal priorities part of the contract? And is the smallest value the most urgent, or the largest? Heapq is a min-heap, so a larger-is-more-urgent priority has to be negated.

The standard way to implement a priority queue is a binary heap, and its trick is that it is a tree stored without any pointers at all. A binary heap is a complete binary tree. Every level is full, except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. Because the shape is so regular, the tree can be laid out level by level in a plain array. The root goes at index zero, its two children at indices one and two, their children at three to six, and so on. Then the links are pure arithmetic. The children of the item at index i are at two i plus one and two i plus two, and its parent is at i minus one, floor-divided by two. The board shows the same heap twice, as a tree and as the array it is actually stored in, with the brackets marking each pair of siblings. The script checks the formulas: index one's children are three and four, holding seven and four, and index five's parent is index two. Completeness keeps the tree as short as possible, with height the floor of log base two of n, and it means the array never has gaps. The ordering rule is the heap invariant. In a min-heap, every parent is less than or equal to each of its children. Following parents upwards always reaches smaller values, so the smallest item is always at the root, index zero. That is all the invariant promises. Siblings can be in either order, and nothing relates the left subtree to the right one. The script confirms that this array is a valid min-heap, but it is not sorted. This is deliberately weaker than the binary search tree property of chapter six. It cannot answer general lookups, but it is much cheaper to restore after a change, which the next section shows.

Both heap operations follow the same plan. Make the change in a way that keeps the shape complete, accept that the order is now broken in one place, and repair it along a single path. To push, append the new item at the end of the array. That is the next free position on the bottom level, so the tree stays complete. Only one thing can now be wrong: the new item may be smaller than its parent. So compare them, and if the new item is smaller, swap them. Repeat from its new position until it is no smaller than its parent or reaches the root. This is called sifting up. The demo prints the array after each push. When one is pushed, it starts at index three, is smaller than its parent five, then smaller than three, and rises all the way to the root. To pop, the minimum is at the root, so take it. To keep the shape complete, move the last item in the array into the root's place. Now the root may be larger than a child. Swap it with the smaller of its two children, and repeat downwards until it is no larger than its children. This is sifting down. Swapping with the smaller child is essential. It puts the smallest of the three values on top, so the invariant holds for both subtrees at once. Swapping with the larger child would put the larger value above the smaller one. Each repair moves along one path between the root and a leaf, so push and pop each cost at most the height, which is logarithmic. The demo pops all six items and they come out in sorted order, using eight swaps in total. That observation, repeated popping produces sorted order, is the idea behind heapsort in section five.

Sometimes all the items are available at once, and we want to turn an existing array into a heap. The obvious way is to push them one at a time. Each push may sift up through the whole height, so that costs n log n. There is a better way, and its analysis is a favourite example of careful counting. Bottom-up construction treats the array as a complete tree already, and repairs it from the bottom up. Every leaf on its own is a valid heap, and leaves make up about half of all nodes, so they need no work at all. Then, from the last internal node backwards to the root, sift each node down. When a node is sifted down, both of its subtrees are already heaps, so the repair is exactly the one from the previous section. The naive analysis says each sift-down costs up to log n, so the total is n log n again. That bound is true, but it is not tight, because it charges every node the full height of the tree. In fact a node at height h can sift down at most h levels, and most nodes are near the bottom. The table on the board does the honest count for a thousand and twenty-three items. Five hundred and twelve leaves cost nothing. Two hundred and fifty-six nodes at height one cost at most one swap each. A hundred and twenty-eight at height two cost at most two, and so on, up to the single root at height nine. The sum of nodes times height is less than n, because the number of nodes halves at each level while the height grows only by one. The script confirms it on a descending input, the worst case. Bottom-up construction makes one thousand and thirteen swaps, while repeated pushing makes eight thousand one hundred and ninety-four. Python's heapify uses the bottom-up method.

If popping a heap repeatedly produces items in sorted order, then a heap gives a sorting algorithm. Heapsort does it in place, inside the original array, with no second array. First, build a max-heap from the whole array using the bottom-up method, which takes linear time. The largest item is now at the root, index zero. Swap it with the last item of the heap. The largest item is now in its final sorted position at the end, so shrink the heap by one to leave it there, and sift the new root down to restore the heap. Repeat. Each round moves the next largest item into place just before the previous one, so the sorted part grows from the back of the array while the heap shrinks at the front. There are n minus one rounds, each costing a logarithmic sift-down, so heapsort is n log n in the worst case. The table on the board compares it with chapter four's algorithms. Like merge sort, heapsort guarantees n log n, but it needs only constant extra space instead of merge sort's linear buffer. Unlike quicksort, it has no quadratic worst case. The costs are elsewhere. Heapsort is not stable. The output sorts five parcels by weight, and the three eight hundred gram parcels, which arrived as two-twenty-one, five-twelve and six hundred, come out in a different order. Swapping the maximum to the end over long distances scrambles ties, as selection sort's swaps did. Heapsort also jumps around the array, reading parents and children far apart in memory, so its locality is poor and it is often slower in practice than quicksort or merge sort. It is the right choice when guaranteed time and no extra memory both matter, and stability does not.

Heaps earn their place in many algorithms, always for the same reason: they deliver the next best item from a set that keeps changing. The first example is choosing the k largest items from a stream, such as the three heaviest parcels of the day. Sorting everything would work, but needs all the data at once and n log n time. Instead, keep a min-heap of the k heaviest seen so far. Its root is the lightest of those, the weakest member of the current top three. For each new parcel, if it is heavier than the root, replace the root with it and sift down. Each step costs log k, so the whole stream costs n log k, and the heap never holds more than k items, however long the stream is. The output agrees with Python's n largest function, which uses the same idea. The second example is merging several sorted lists into one, such as the parcel lists from three depots, each already sorted. A heap holds the current front item of each list. Pop the smallest, output it, and push the next item from the same list. For k lists holding n items in total, that costs n log k. Heapq's merge function does exactly this, and it is lazy, producing items one at a time, so it can merge files too large to fit in memory. The third family is scheduling. Event-driven simulations keep a heap of future events ordered by time and always process the earliest next. Job schedulers keep a heap of tasks ordered by deadline or priority. And one of the most important graph algorithms, Dijkstra's shortest paths in chapter ten, is at heart a heap-driven schedule: it repeatedly settles whichever place is currently closest.

Priorities do not always stay fixed. A parcel can be escalated while it is waiting, and the queue has to reflect the change. In a heap, the entry is somewhere in the middle of the array, and there are two standard designs for changing it. The first is an indexed heap. Alongside the array, it keeps a map from each item to its current index, and every swap during a sift updates that map. To change a priority, look up the item's index, change the priority in place, and sift up or down as needed. That costs logarithmic time and keeps exactly one entry per item. It is efficient, but every operation must maintain the index map correctly, and Python's heapq module does not provide it. The second design is lazy, and it needs nothing beyond heapq. To change a priority, simply push a new entry with the new priority, and record the item's live priority in a dict. The old entry stays in the heap, now stale. When popping, check each entry against the dict, and quietly discard any entry whose priority is no longer the live one. The script escalates P one-oh-four from five to one. The heap now holds four entries for three parcels. Popping returns the parcels in the right order, with P one-oh-four first, and the stale entry is left behind, never returned. The cost of laziness is memory and some extra pops. The heap holds one entry per update, not per item, so memory grows with the number of updates. Pops occasionally discard stale entries, but each entry is popped at most once, so the total work stays logarithmic per entry. The table summarises the trade-off. This same choice will reappear in Dijkstra's algorithm, where the lazy design is usually the practical one in Python.

This chapter is about searching through choices, and its main tool is recursion. Before using recursion to explore, it is worth being precise about why a recursive function is correct, because the reasons are the same ones that made loops correct in chapter one. A recursive function carries three obligations. First, a contract: what every call receives and what it returns, stated once for all calls. The function on the board takes a route, which is either a single parcel identifier or a list of routes, and returns the total weight. Second, a base case: inputs small enough to answer directly, here a single identifier, whose weight is looked up. Third, progress: every recursive call is on an input strictly smaller than the current one, here one element of the list. Because the input cannot shrink forever, the recursion must reach base cases and stop. With those three in place, the reasoning is simple. Assume the recursive calls meet the contract, and check that this call then meets it too. If each part's total is right, adding them gives the right total for the whole list. That assumption is not circular. It is induction on the size of the input, the same argument as the loop invariant's maintenance step. It helps to picture the call state. Every call that has started but not yet returned has its own frame, with its own route and depth. The output is indented by depth, so the nesting is visible. The route holds lists three deep, and at the deepest point four frames are active at once. Finally, check the boundary. An empty list is a valid route under the contract. Its sum has no terms, so its total is zero, and the code handles it without any special case.

Some problems have no clever shortcut, at least none we know of, and the only reliable method is to consider every combination of choices. The delivery planner meets one immediately: assigning parcels to vans so that no van is overloaded. To search every combination without missing any or repeating any, we organise the choices as a tree, called a state-space tree. Each level of the tree fixes one decision. At the top, nothing is decided. The first level decides which van carries parcel one, the second level decides parcel two, and so on. Each internal node is a partial plan, and each leaf is a complete plan. The board draws the tree for two parcels and two vans: two choices for the first parcel, two for the second, four leaves. In general, with two choices at each of n levels, there are two to the n leaves. The script generates the tree for three parcels and prints its eight leaves. The step at each node, listing the possible next choices, is called candidate generation. The search then recurses on each candidate in turn. So the recursion is a depth-first walk of the state-space tree: it goes down one path to a leaf, backs up, and tries the next choice. One important point: the tree is never actually stored. At any moment, only the current path from the root exists, held in the call stack and in the chosen list, so the memory needed is proportional to the depth, not to the number of leaves. Every search in this chapter is a walk of some state-space tree, and its size is its cost. The remaining sections are about walking it correctly, enumerating it without duplicates, and cutting away subtrees that cannot contain an answer.

A state-space search needs to remember the current partial plan as it walks the tree. The standard technique, backtracking, keeps a single mutable state for the whole search, and changes it as it goes. The pattern has three steps at every node. Choose: apply one decision to the state, here adding a parcel's weight to one van's load and recording which van. Explore: recurse to decide the next parcel. Undo: reverse the choice exactly, removing the weight and the record, so the next candidate starts from the same state. The code also checks feasibility before choosing. If adding the parcel would push a van over six thousand grams, that branch is never entered at all. Over four parcels and two vans, the search finds four feasible plans. The alternative is to copy the state at every step, passing a fresh list to each recursive call. That is simpler to get right, because no call can damage another's state, but it allocates new lists constantly. The copying version on the board builds twenty-eight lists to find the same four plans. For deep searches with large states, copying can dominate the running time. There is one place where copying is required: a plan that must outlive the search. When a leaf is reached, the current plan is copied into the results, because the shared list will keep changing afterwards. Storing the list itself would leave the results full of references to one list, which by the end of the search is empty. The aliasing lesson again. Backtracking's correctness rests on an invariant: after each recursive call returns, the state is exactly as it was before the call. Every choose must be matched by an undo, in reverse order, including on every path that returns early.

Most exhaustive searches enumerate one of three standard families of candidates, and it is worth knowing how to generate each and how many there are. The first family is subsets. Each item is either taken or left, so n items have two to the n subsets. A compact way to enumerate them uses a bit mask: an integer whose bit k says whether item k is taken. Counting the integers from zero up to two to the n, minus one, visits every subset exactly once, with no recursion at all. The output lists the eight subsets of three depots in mask order. Bit masks are cheap for small n, but remember chapter two's point: an integer with many bits is no longer a single machine step. The second family is permutations, orderings of all the items. Choose which item goes first, then recursively order the rest. There are n factorial permutations. Every possible order of visiting n delivery stops is one, which is why route planning grows so quickly. The third family is combinations, subsets of a fixed size k, such as which two of three vans to send. Their number is n choose k, n factorial divided by k factorial and n minus k factorial. The script checks its hand-written generators against Python's itertools module and the counting formulas, and all agree. In practice, use itertools: it is correct and fast. Writing the generators by hand matters for understanding, and for adding pruning, which itertools cannot do. The table on the board carries the real lesson. At twenty items, there are about a million subsets, which is fine. There are two point four times ten to the eighteen orderings, which no computer will ever finish. Knowing which family a problem enumerates tells you, before writing any code, whether exhaustive search is even possible.

Enumeration has a trap when items repeat. Suppose a route must visit three stops, two of them at the North depot. Naive permutation treats the two North stops as different items, so every route appears twice, once with each North stop first. The output shows six results for only three distinct routes. With more repeats the waste grows quickly. If one value appears k times, every distinct arrangement is generated k factorial times over. A tempting fix is to collect the results in a set. That does remove the duplicates from the answer, but it does not remove the work. The search still walks every duplicate subtree in full before throwing its results away. The better fix is to generate each distinct answer exactly once, which is called canonical enumeration. The rule is short. First, sort the items, so that equal items are next to each other. Then, at each level of the recursion, skip any choice whose value equals the previous choice at that same level. The reasoning is that two equal choices at the same level lead to identical subtrees: everything below them is the same set of remaining items. So exploring the first copy covers both, and skipping the second loses nothing. The output shows the canonical version producing each of the three routes once. The same idea applies to subsets and combinations with repeated items, and it generalises: whenever two branches of a search are equivalent, by symmetry or by equal values, choose one canonical representative and skip the rest. For example, when assigning parcels to two identical vans, putting the first parcel in van A or van B gives mirror-image subtrees, so it is enough to place it in van A. Canonical rules are a kind of pruning, and like all pruning, they must be proved not to discard any distinct answer.

Exhaustive search is only practical if large parts of the state-space tree can be skipped. Skipping a subtree is called pruning, and a prune is sound only if it can never throw away an answer we need. There are two classic kinds of sound prune. The first is feasibility. If a choice already breaks a constraint, such as exceeding a van's capacity, no completion of that branch can be valid, so the branch ends immediately. The second is a bound, used when searching for the best answer, not just any answer. The search keeps the best plan found so far, called the incumbent. At each node, it computes an optimistic estimate of the best this branch could possibly achieve. Here, that is the current load plus every remaining parcel. If even that optimistic total cannot beat the incumbent, the whole subtree is pruned. This is branch and bound. The script searches for the heaviest load that fits in nine thousand grams. Without pruning it visits ninety-eight nodes. With the bound, it visits thirty-eight, and finds the same best load, eight thousand seven hundred. Notice the distinction between the incumbent and the optimum. At any moment during the search, the incumbent is just the best found so far. It is only proved optimal when the search finishes, because only then has every unpruned branch been examined. The lower half of the board shows what happens when a prune is not sound. This search decides that once a parcel fits, it will never try leaving it out. That sounds reasonable, and every plan it returns is feasible. But it returns eight thousand three hundred, while the true optimum, computed by checking all sixty-four subsets, is eight thousand seven hundred. The optimal plan was inside a subtree the rule discarded. Every prune therefore needs its own small proof.

An exhaustive search runs into two separate limits, and it is important not to confuse them. The first is depth: how many decisions deep the search goes. In a recursive search, each level holds a frame on the call stack, and CPython stops at a recursion limit of one thousand frames by default. A search that must make five thousand decisions in sequence fails with a recursion error, regardless of how fast the computer is. The fix for depth is mechanical. Replace the recursion with a loop and an explicit stack of pending states. The loop pops a state, processes it, and pushes the states that would have been recursive calls. It explores the tree in the same order, and the stack holds exactly what the call stack would have held, but it lives in an ordinary list, so it has no recursion limit. The script follows a path five thousand deep this way without any trouble. The second limit is breadth: how many nodes the tree contains. Here no trick helps. The script counts the two to the twenty leaves of a full subset tree, just over a million, which finishes in about a second. Two to the forty is a million times more, which would take weeks. Two to the sixty is a million times more again, longer than any computer has existed. Replacing recursion with iteration changes how depth is stored. It does not reduce the number of nodes at all. So when exhaustive search is too slow, the remedies are the ones from this chapter and the next ones: prune sound subtrees, avoid duplicate work with canonical rules, and above all, find a better formulation of the problem. Greedy choices in chapter eleven and dynamic programming in chapter twelve both start from exactly that question.

Lists capture sequence and trees capture hierarchy. Many relationships fit neither: roads between depots, dependencies between tasks, connections in a network. The general model is a graph, a set of vertices together with a set of edges, each edge connecting two vertices. Building a graph model involves a few choices, and making them correctly is part of solving the problem. An edge can be undirected, meaning it works both ways, like a road usable in either direction. In code, an undirected edge is usually stored in both directions, so each depot lists the other as a neighbour. The output confirms it: Hub lists North, and North lists Hub. An edge can be directed, like a one-way street, or like a dependency, where task a must happen before task b. An edge can carry a weight, a number such as the minutes needed to drive it. And some problems need a multigraph, which allows several edges between the same pair of vertices, such as a main road and a toll road between Hub and North. The board shows the depot road network: eight depots and seven roads, undirected and unweighted for now. The number of edges at a vertex is its degree, and Hub has degree three. Notice that Airfield and Annex connect to each other but to nothing else. The graph has two separate pieces, which will matter for traversal. This chapter uses two different graphs, and the difference is the point. Roads between depots form an undirected graph. Task dependencies, such as weighing a parcel before labelling it, form a directed graph. The same algorithms apply to both, but the questions differ. Lists and trees were special cases of graphs all along. What general graphs add is cycles and multiple paths between the same two vertices, and the algorithms in this chapter exist to handle exactly that.

A graph has to be stored before it can be searched, and the two standard representations make different operations cheap, just as the sequence representations did in chapter three. An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours. The board shows it for the depot network. Its memory is proportional to the number of vertices plus the number of edges. For seven undirected roads, each stored in both directions, that is fourteen list entries. Listing the neighbours of a vertex is as fast as possible: it costs exactly the vertex's degree. Asking whether one particular edge exists means scanning a neighbour list. An adjacency matrix is a table with one row and one column per vertex, where the cell for u and v is one if the edge exists and zero otherwise. The board shows the top-left corner of it. Its memory is the number of vertices squared, sixty-four cells here, almost all of them zeros, because each depot connects to only a few others. Testing whether Hub and Port are connected is a single lookup. But listing Hub's neighbours means scanning its whole row, all eight cells, even though only three are ones. The script measures these differences directly. The choice should follow the operations the program needs. Most real networks are sparse, meaning each vertex connects to only a few others, and most algorithms in the next two chapters mostly ask for neighbours. For them, an adjacency list is the right default, and it is what the rest of the course uses. A matrix suits dense graphs, where most pairs are connected, and algorithms that constantly ask whether a specific edge exists, such as the all-pairs shortest path method of chapter ten.

The first way to explore a graph is breadth-first search. It works outward from a starting vertex in layers. First every vertex one hop away, then every vertex two hops away, and so on. The engine is a queue, the first-in, first-out structure from chapter three. The search starts with only the source in the queue, at distance zero. It repeatedly takes the vertex at the front of the queue and looks at its neighbours. Any neighbour not yet visited gets a distance one greater than the current vertex, records the current vertex as its parent, and joins the back of the queue. A vertex is marked visited the moment it is first queued, so each vertex enters the queue once, and each adjacency list is scanned once. With an adjacency list, the whole search costs time proportional to the vertices plus the edges. The board shows the layers from North. Hub and East are one hop away. West is two, South three, and Port four. Because the queue serves vertices strictly in order of distance, the first time a vertex is reached is by a shortest route, measured in hops. The parent pointers record that route. Following them backwards from Port, through South, West and Hub to North, and reversing, reconstructs a shortest path, which the output prints. The output also shows that Airfield is never reached. It lies in a different component of the graph, and no search from North can find it. The guarantee needs to be stated carefully. Breadth-first search finds paths with the fewest edges. That is the shortest path only when every edge counts the same. If roads take different numbers of minutes, a route with more hops can be faster, and breadth-first search will not find it. Weighted shortest paths need the methods of chapter ten.

Depth-first search explores in the opposite spirit. Instead of layers, it follows one path as deep as it can go, and only when it reaches a dead end does it back up and try the next branch. It is the backtracking walk of chapter eight, applied to a graph, with one difference: a vertex that has been visited is never entered again. The useful information comes from a clock. The clock ticks when a vertex is first discovered, and ticks again when the search has finished with it, meaning all of its descendants are done. Between those two moments, the vertex is active: it is on the current path. The board shows the task graph with each task's discovery and finish times. Weigh is discovered at one and finished at eight. Inside that interval, label is discovered at two and finished at seven, so label was explored entirely within weigh. Intervals either nest or are disjoint, which is how depth-first search reveals the structure of a graph. With these times we can classify each edge by where it leads. A tree edge leads to a newly discovered vertex. A back edge leads to a vertex that is still active, an ancestor on the current path, and that closes a cycle. A cross edge leads to a vertex that is already finished. On the board, sort to load is a cross edge: load was finished at six, long before sort was discovered at ten. In a directed graph, the presence of any back edge is exactly the presence of a cycle. One search from one start may not reach everything, so depth-first search restarts from every vertex not yet discovered. Here it starts again at scan, and then at inspect. The total cost is still proportional to vertices plus edges. And the order in which vertices finish turns out to be the key to the next two sections.

Traversal answers two basic questions about a graph. The first is reachability: which vertices can be reached from which? In an undirected graph, the vertices split into connected components, groups where every vertex reaches every other, with no edges between groups. Finding them takes one idea: start a search from any vertex not yet seen, mark everything it reaches as one component, and repeat until every vertex is seen. Each restart finds exactly one new component. The components script does this for the depot roads and finds two, the six main depots, and Airfield with Annex. Once components are known, asking whether u reaches v is just asking whether they share a component. The second question is whether a directed graph has a cycle. That matters a great deal for task dependencies, because a cycle of dependencies can never be scheduled. From the previous section, a directed graph has a cycle exactly when depth-first search finds a back edge, an edge to a vertex that is still active on the current path. So the search tracks three states: unvisited, on the current path, and finished. A common mistake is to track only one flag, visited or not, and report a cycle whenever an edge leads to a visited vertex. The board shows why that fails. In the diamond, a has edges to b and c, and both lead to d. The search goes a, b, d and finishes them. Then it goes to c, which has an edge to d. D is visited, so the single-flag test reports a cycle. But there is no cycle. D is finished, not on the current path. The output confirms that the path-state version answers correctly for both the diamond and a true loop, while the single flag gets the diamond wrong. In an undirected graph the rule is different again, since every edge leads straight back to its parent.

A set of tasks with dependencies needs a schedule: an order in which every task comes after all of its prerequisites. Such an order is called a topological order, and it exists exactly when the dependency graph has no cycle. Kahn's algorithm constructs one directly. First, count each task's in-degree, the number of prerequisites it is still waiting on. The table on the board shows the starting counts. Weigh, scan and inspect have none, so they are ready immediately. Label and sort wait on one task each. Load and dispatch wait on two. The algorithm keeps a queue of ready tasks. It repeatedly takes one, appends it to the order, and then, for each task that depended on it, decreases that task's count by one. Any task whose count reaches zero has all its prerequisites done, so it joins the ready queue. Each task and each dependency is handled once, so the cost is proportional to vertices plus edges. The output gives the order weigh, scan, inspect, label, sort, load, dispatch. It is not the only valid order. Any order that respects every edge is a correct schedule, and different ready queues would produce different ones. The real value of Kahn's algorithm shows when the dependencies are wrong. The script adds a dependency from dispatch back to scan, which creates a cycle: scan before sort, before load, before dispatch, before scan. Now four tasks wait on each other forever, and their counts never reach zero. The algorithm notices that its order is shorter than the task list, and reports exactly which tasks are stuck. That is far better than a scheduler that loops forever or silently skips work. Depth-first search gives an alternative method: reversing the order in which tasks finish also produces a topological order, because every task finishes after everything it leads to.

In a directed graph, reachability is not symmetric. One-way streets may let you drive from A to D but not back. The right notion of a group is a strongly connected component: a maximal set of vertices in which every vertex can reach every other along directed edges. The board shows six stops joined by one-way streets. A, B and C form a loop, so each reaches the others, and they form one component. D and E reach each other, a second component. F can be reached but leads nowhere, so it is a component on its own. Every vertex belongs to exactly one strongly connected component. Finding them takes a clever use of depth-first search. This course uses Kosaraju's algorithm, because its reasoning is the easiest to see. It makes two passes. The first pass runs depth-first search on the graph and records the order in which vertices finish. The second pass reverses every edge, then runs depth-first search on the reversed graph, taking start vertices in reverse finishing order, latest finish first. Each search in the second pass collects exactly one component. Why does that work? The vertex that finishes last lies in a component that nothing else points into, a source among the components. In the reversed graph, that component has no way out, so the search from it collects that component and nothing else. Removing it, the same argument applies to the next. Both passes are linear, so the whole algorithm costs vertices plus edges. Shrinking each component to a single vertex gives a graph called the condensation, and it is always acyclic, since any cycle between components would merge them into one. Here it is the chain from A, B and C, to D and E, to F, which can be processed in topological order like any other dependency graph.

Every traversal in this chapter has been described as costing vertices plus edges. That figure assumes an adjacency list, and it is worth seeing what happens otherwise. The script builds a sparse random graph of a thousand vertices and about three thousand edges, stored both ways, and counts the steps a traversal takes. With an adjacency list, each vertex is visited once and each of its neighbours is examined once, about four thousand steps in all. With an adjacency matrix, finding a vertex's neighbours means scanning its whole row of a thousand cells, whether the edges are there or not. That is over a million steps, two hundred and fifty times more, to do exactly the same search. The memory follows the same pattern, as the table shows. For sparse graphs, the list wins on every count that traversal cares about. Traversals also need space of their own. Both searches keep a visited mark and a parent for each vertex, which is linear in the number of vertices. Breadth-first search's queue can hold a whole layer, and depth-first search's stack a whole path, each up to the number of vertices in the worst case. A recursive depth-first search keeps that path on the call stack, so on a long chain in Python it runs into the recursion limit from chapter two. Choosing between the two searches is mostly about the question being asked. For the fewest hops, or anything defined by layers, use breadth-first search. For cycles, finishing order, topological order and components, use depth-first search, whose discovery and finish structure carries the information. When paths can be long, write depth-first search with an explicit stack. Next, edges get weights, and both searches need upgrading to find the cheapest routes rather than the shortest in hops.

Chapter nine found shortest routes by counting hops. Now roads have lengths, measured in minutes, and the fewest hops is no longer the fastest route. Every algorithm in this chapter is built from a single operation called relaxation, so it is worth understanding it on its own first. Each vertex keeps a distance estimate: the length of the best route to it found so far. The source starts at zero and every other vertex starts at infinity, meaning no route is known yet. Each vertex also keeps a predecessor, the vertex just before it on that best route, so the route itself can be reconstructed by following predecessors backwards, exactly as with parents in breadth-first search. An estimate is always an upper bound. Whenever it is finite, a real route of that length exists, so the true shortest distance can only be smaller or equal. Relaxing an edge from u to v with weight w asks one question: is the best route to u, followed by this edge, better than the best route to v known so far? If the distance to u plus w is less than the distance to v, both the distance and the predecessor of v are updated. Otherwise nothing changes. The script tries four relaxations around North, East and Hub. North to Hub sets Hub to twelve. North to East sets East to four. Then East to Hub would give four plus nine, thirteen, which is worse than twelve, so it changes nothing. And Airfield is never touched. Its estimate stays infinite and its predecessor stays empty, which is the honest answer when no route exists. All of the algorithms that follow, for DAGs, Dijkstra, Bellman and Ford, are different strategies for choosing which edges to relax, and in what order, so that the estimates become exact.

The simplest case is a graph with no cycles, a DAG, such as one-way legs of a delivery run that never return to an earlier point. Here a single pass is enough, provided the vertices are processed in the right order. Take the vertices in topological order, the order from chapter nine, and relax every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once. That is all. Each vertex and each edge is handled once, so the cost is proportional to vertices plus edges. The correctness argument is short. Topological order means every edge points forward. So by the time a vertex u is processed, every edge leading into u comes from an earlier vertex, and has already been relaxed. Every possible route into u has therefore been considered, and its distance is already final when its own outgoing edges are used. Notice that nothing in this argument cares whether weights are negative. Without cycles, negative weights cause no trouble at all. The board shows the run. From the depot, the direct leg to A costs five. But B is processed first, at a distance of three, and its leg to A costs one, so A's estimate drops to four, via B. C then gets ten, by way of A, and the drop point twelve. Following the predecessors back from the drop point gives the route depot, B, A, C, drop. The same method finds longest paths too, simply by maximising instead of minimising. In a project schedule, where edges are task durations and dependencies, the longest path is the critical path, the chain of tasks that determines the earliest finishing time. That is easy in a DAG, though for general graphs with cycles, longest simple paths turn out to be a hard problem, a theme of chapter fourteen.

When the graph has cycles, there is no topological order to follow. Dijkstra's algorithm replaces it with a different order: settle vertices in increasing order of distance from the source. It keeps a min-heap of distance and vertex pairs, starting with the source at zero. It repeatedly pops the closest vertex not yet finished. At that moment, the vertex's distance is declared final. Then it relaxes the vertex's outgoing edges, and pushes any improved estimate onto the heap. This version is lazy, exactly as in chapter seven. Instead of updating an entry inside the heap, it pushes a new one and skips stale entries when they surface. The output shows one stale entry skipped. On the depot roads, starting from North, the depots are finalised in order: North at zero, East at four, Hub at twelve, West at nineteen, South at twenty-five, and Port at thirty-four. Port is reached via East, four plus thirty, which narrowly beats the route via South, twenty-five plus ten. With a binary heap, each edge causes at most one push and each push or pop costs log V, so the total is V plus E, times log V. The key step, declaring a popped distance final, depends on an assumption: no edge weight is negative. If all weights are nonnegative, any other route to the popped vertex would have to pass through a vertex that is at least as far away, and could only add to that distance. With a negative edge, that argument fails. The small graph on the board shows it. A reaches C directly in two, and reaches B in five. Dijkstra pops C at two and finalises it before ever looking at B. But B's edge to C has weight minus four, so the route through B costs one. The output confirms Dijkstra's wrong answer.

Some problems genuinely have negative weights, such as a leg of a route that earns a credit or a refund. Bellman-Ford handles them, at a higher price. It simply relaxes every edge in the graph, and repeats that whole pass V minus one times. That costs V times E. Why V minus one passes? After the first pass, every shortest route that uses at most one edge has been found. After the second, every one using at most two edges, and so on, because each pass extends the best known routes by one more edge. A shortest route never needs to repeat a vertex, so it uses at most V minus one edges, and after that many passes every distance is exact. The first line of output uses a graph where the leg from C to B carries a credit of minus six. The route from Hub through C to B costs eight minus six, which is two, beating the direct route through A at seven, and Port then follows at four. This is exactly the kind of answer Dijkstra cannot be trusted to give. Negative edges raise a deeper problem: a negative cycle. In the second graph, going from A to B and back to A costs a total of minus one. Every lap round that cycle makes the route cheaper, so for any destination reachable through it, there is no shortest route at all. Its distance is effectively minus infinity. Bellman-Ford detects this. If any edge can still be relaxed after V minus one passes, some cycle is negative. The code then marks every vertex reachable from such an edge. The output reports A, B and Port as minus infinity. C is still eight, because the cycle cannot reach it, and Annex is still infinite, because nothing reaches Annex at all. So a reachable negative cycle only spoils the destinations it can actually reach.

Some questions need distances between every pair of depots, for instance to build a travel-time table for the dispatch office. One option is to run a single-source algorithm from every vertex. Another is the Floyd-Warshall algorithm, which is short enough to remember and works directly on a table. It starts from a matrix of direct distances: the road length where a road exists, infinity where none does, and zero on the diagonal. Then it considers each vertex k in turn as a possible intermediate stop. For every pair i and j, it asks whether going from i to k and then from k to j is shorter than the best route from i to j known so far, and if so, updates the table. That is three nested loops, so the cost is V cubed. The order of the loops matters, and it comes with an invariant. After the stage for k, every entry of the table is the shortest route that uses only the first k vertices as intermediate stops. When the stage for the last vertex is complete, every vertex is allowed, so every entry is exact. That only works if k is the outer loop. Putting it inside the others breaks the invariant and gives wrong answers. The output shows the finished table for four depots. North and West have no direct road, yet the table gives nineteen minutes, travelling via East and Hub. Floyd-Warshall allows negative edges, and if a negative cycle exists, some diagonal entry ends up below zero, which is a convenient check. The table on the board summarises the choice. Floyd-Warshall's V cubed is simple and suits small or dense graphs. For large sparse graphs with nonnegative weights, running Dijkstra from each vertex is much faster.

Spanning trees answer a different question from shortest paths, and it is important not to confuse them. Suppose the planner wants to keep a road network that connects every depot, and maintaining each road costs its length. The cheapest such network is a minimum spanning tree. A spanning tree connects all V vertices using exactly V minus one edges, so it has no cycles and no redundant roads. A minimum spanning tree has the least total weight among all spanning trees. The left tree on the board is one for the depot roads, with a total of thirty-six minutes of road. If the graph is disconnected, no single tree can span it, and the answer is a spanning forest, one tree per component. Two properties drive every minimum spanning tree algorithm. The cut property: divide the vertices into two groups in any way, and the lightest edge crossing between the groups belongs to some minimum spanning tree. The cycle property: on any cycle, the heaviest edge is not needed, since the others already connect its ends more cheaply. The right tree on the board is the shortest-path tree from North, the tree formed by Dijkstra's predecessors. Its total road length is fifty-nine, much more than thirty-six, because it is built for a different goal. It guarantees that every depot is reached from North by the fastest possible route. The minimum spanning tree guarantees the cheapest network overall, but some routes in it are long. For example, Port is reached through the whole chain of depots. Neither tree solves a third problem: a single tour that visits every depot and returns, which is the travelling salesperson problem. Unlike the two trees, no efficient exact algorithm is known for it, as chapter fourteen explains.

Building a spanning tree edge by edge needs a fast answer to one question: are these two depots already connected by the edges chosen so far? The disjoint-set union structure, also called union-find, answers exactly that, while connections keep being added. It supports two operations. Find returns the representative of an item's set. Union merges the sets containing two items, and reports false if they were already in the same set, which is how a spanning tree algorithm detects that an edge would close a cycle. Internally, each set is a tree of parent pointers. Each item points to a parent, and the root points to itself and serves as the representative. Find follows parent pointers up to the root. Union finds both roots and makes one the parent of the other. Without care, these trees can become long chains, just like the unbalanced search trees of chapter six. Two simple heuristics prevent that. Union by size always hangs the smaller tree under the root of the larger one, so trees stay shallow. Path compression makes find do some housekeeping: after locating the root, it points every node on the path directly at the root, so later finds are almost instant. The demo performs four unions. The fourth, joining West and North, returns false, because they are already connected through East and Hub. Before that, West had been placed under Hub. The find for West compresses its path, and afterwards West points directly at North, as the printed parents show. South was never joined, so it remains a root on its own. With both heuristics together, the amortised cost per operation is nearly constant. It is bounded by an extremely slow-growing function, the inverse Ackermann function, which is below five for any input that could exist in practice.

Two classic algorithms build minimum spanning trees, and both are greedy: they repeatedly take the locally cheapest safe edge. Kruskal's algorithm sorts all the edges by weight and considers them from lightest to heaviest. Each edge is added unless it would connect two depots that are already connected, since that would close a cycle. Union-find answers that question in nearly constant time, so the total cost is dominated by sorting the edges, E log E. Because Kruskal never needs a starting point, it handles a disconnected graph naturally. The demo adds a separate Airfield and Annex road, and Kruskal returns six edges for eight vertices, a spanning forest of two trees. Prim's algorithm grows a single tree from a starting vertex. At every step it adds the lightest edge that connects the tree to a vertex not yet in it. A heap holds the candidate edges crossing from the tree to the outside, and as in Dijkstra, stale entries, edges whose far end has already joined, are skipped when they surface. With this lazy heap, the cost is also E log E. Prim only ever spans the component containing its start. Both algorithms are correct for the same reason, the cut property from section six. Every edge Kruskal adds is the lightest edge crossing the cut between its endpoint's current group and everything else, and every edge Prim adds is the lightest edge crossing the cut between the tree and the rest. So every edge either algorithm adds belongs to some minimum spanning tree. The output shows both reaching the same total of thirty-six. When weights tie, there can be several different minimum spanning trees, but their total weight is always the same. The next chapter asks when greedy choices like these can be trusted in general.

Chapter eight searched every combination, and pruning helped only so much. Greedy algorithms take the opposite approach. They build an answer one step at a time, and at each step they take whichever choice looks best right now, never reconsidering it. Every greedy algorithm has three parts. Feasibility defines what counts as a valid answer. The objective defines what makes one valid answer better than another. And the greedy rule is the local choice made at each step. The appeal is obvious. A greedy algorithm usually needs one sort and one pass, n log n in total, with no search tree, no backtracking, and very little code. The danger is just as obvious once stated. A locally best choice can rule out a globally better answer, and because the choice is never undone, the algorithm cannot recover. So every greedy algorithm needs a proof, and the script shows why. The task is to make up a postage amount with as few stamps as possible, using the rule: always take the largest stamp that still fits. For stamps of one, two, five and ten, an amount of eighteen becomes ten, five, two and one, four stamps, which brute force confirms is optimal. Now change the stamp set to one, three and four, and the amount to six. The same rule takes four first, then has to add one and one, three stamps. But three plus three uses only two. Nothing about the rule changed. What changed is the problem instance, and with it, whether the local choice is safe. That is the central lesson of this chapter. Greedy correctness is a property of a particular problem, never of the greedy idea itself, and the next section shows the standard way to prove it.

The standard way to prove a greedy rule correct is called an exchange argument. The idea is to take any optimal answer and show that it can be transformed, step by step, into the greedy answer without ever getting worse. If that is always possible, the greedy answer is optimal too. Here is a problem where it works. The planner wants to load as many parcels as possible into one van with a capacity of six thousand grams. The objective is the count of parcels, not their total weight. The greedy rule is to sort the parcels by weight and take them lightest first, as long as each one still fits. The proof runs as follows. Take any optimal loading O, and compare it with the greedy loading, both sorted by weight. Find the first position where they differ. There, greedy took some parcel g, while O has a different parcel o. Because greedy always takes the lightest remaining parcel, g weighs no more than o. So swap them: take o out of O and put g in. The total weight cannot increase, so the load still fits, and the number of parcels is unchanged, so it is still optimal. The new optimal answer agrees with greedy for one more position. Repeat the swap until there are no differences left. Then the greedy answer has been reached without losing value, which proves it is optimal. The code on the board also checks the claim on two hundred random instances, comparing greedy with brute force over every subset, and they agree every time. It is worth being clear about what each piece contributes. The tests are evidence, and they would catch a mistake in the argument or the code. But only the argument covers every possible instance, including all the ones never tested. That is the same division of labour as in chapter one.

The classic greedy success story is interval scheduling. One loading dock receives requests for time slots, each with a start and a finish, and two slots conflict if they overlap. The goal is to accept as many slots as possible. Several greedy rules sound reasonable. Accept the slot that starts earliest. Accept the shortest slot, since it blocks the least time. Or accept the slot that finishes earliest. The script tries all three on the eleven slots drawn on the board, and checks them against brute force. Earliest start accepts only three, because a long slot starting at time zero blocks everything else. Shortest first matches the optimum of four on this instance, but a three-slot example shows it failing: a short slot overlapping two longer, compatible ones is accepted, and blocks both. Only earliest finish matches brute force on both instances. On the board, the four slots it chooses are highlighted. The exchange argument explains why it is always safe. The slot that finishes first leaves the dock free as early as possible. Take any optimal schedule, and replace its first slot with the earliest-finishing slot. That slot ends no later than the one it replaced, so it cannot conflict with anything else in the schedule, and the count is unchanged. Now the problem repeats on the slots that start after the chosen one finishes, and the same argument applies again. The algorithm is a sort by finishing time followed by one pass, taking each slot that starts after the last accepted slot finishes, n log n in total. Notice how precisely the result depends on the objective. Every slot counts the same here. The section after next changes that one assumption, and the rule stops working.

Huffman coding applies the greedy idea to compression. Suppose the dispatch log records which depot each scan came from, and North appears far more often than Port. A fixed-length code spends the same number of bits on every symbol, three bits for six depots. A better code gives frequent symbols short codes and rare symbols long ones. To be decodable, the code must be a prefix code: no symbol's code is the beginning of another's. Then a stream of bits can be read from the start, and each symbol is recognised the moment its last bit arrives. Every prefix code corresponds to a binary tree, with the symbols at the leaves and each code spelling out the path from the root, zero for left and one for right. The board shows the tree Huffman's algorithm builds. Its greedy rule is simple. Put every symbol in a heap, weighted by its frequency. Repeatedly remove the two rarest trees and merge them under a new parent whose weight is their sum. The first merge joins P and H into a tree of weight fourteen. When one tree remains, it is the code tree. Because the rarest symbols are merged first, they end up deepest, with long codes such as one one zero zero for P, while North, the most frequent, gets the single bit zero. An exchange argument proves this is optimal: in some optimal tree, the two rarest symbols can be swapped into the deepest pair of sibling leaves without increasing the cost, and the same reasoning repeats on the merged problem. For these hundred scans, Huffman coding uses two hundred and twenty-four bits, against three hundred with fixed three-bit codes. The model has limits worth stating. It is optimal among codes that encode one symbol at a time, for fixed, known frequencies, and it ignores any context between symbols.

A proof of a greedy rule is a proof for one precise formulation of a problem. Change the formulation even slightly, and the rule can fail. The cleanest example is to give interval scheduling weights. Each slot at the dock now carries a value, the number of parcels it moves, and the goal is the greatest total value rather than the greatest number of slots. The board shows four slots. Three short ones are each worth two, and one long one, overlapping all of them, is worth ten. Earliest finish behaves exactly as before. It accepts the three short slots, which are compatible, for a total value of six. But the long slot alone is worth ten, as the brute-force check confirms. It is worth seeing precisely where the proof breaks. The exchange argument swapped the earliest-finishing slot into an optimal schedule and argued that the count did not drop. It never needed to compare values, because every slot counted as one. With values, swapping in the earliest-finishing slot can throw out a slot worth far more, and nothing in the argument prevents that. So the rule was never safe in general. It was safe for the unweighted problem. The practical lessons are these. A proof for one formulation says nothing about another, so whenever an objective or constraint changes, the greedy rule has to be re-justified. Before attempting a proof, look for a counterexample, using small, deliberately constructed inputs that set the rule against itself, as this one does. And when the counterexamples win, the problem usually needs an approach that keeps more information than a single greedy choice. Weighted interval scheduling and the zero-one knapsack problem are both solved exactly by dynamic programming, the subject of the next chapter.

This chapter has a precursor in chapter ten. Kruskal's and Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithms, and Dijkstra's shortest paths, are all greedy, and each rests on its own proof. The script makes the spanning tree case concrete. It runs Kruskal's algorithm on the depot roads and, for every edge it takes, finds the cut between the group on one side and everything else, and checks whether the edge is the lightest one crossing that cut. Every taken edge passes. The three skipped edges would each close a cycle. That is the cut property at work. Each greedy step is safe because it is the lightest crossing edge of some cut, and the lightest crossing edge of any cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree. The table on the board collects the greedy algorithms in this course, each with the argument that justifies it. Kruskal and Prim rely on the cut property. Dijkstra relies on nonnegative weights, which make the closest unfinished vertex's distance final. Interval scheduling, Huffman coding and the most-parcels rule rely on exchange arguments. The pattern is always the same: a local rule, plus a reason why the local choice can be extended to an optimal answer. So when should you reach for a greedy algorithm? When the problem suggests a natural local rule, and you can either prove it with an exchange or cut argument, or at least search hard for small counterexamples and fail to find one. If the rule fails, the usual next steps are a richer formulation that keeps more state, which is dynamic programming in the next chapter, or exhaustive search with pruning from chapter eight. And remember what greedy is. It is a design approach that is correct for some problems. It is not a way of making any algorithm faster.

Chapter eleven ended with problems where no single local choice is safe. Dynamic programming handles them by keeping more information: instead of committing to one choice, it computes the best answer to every relevant subproblem, and then chooses among them. Two conditions make this work. The first is optimal substructure: an optimal answer to the whole problem can be built from optimal answers to smaller subproblems. The second is overlapping subproblems: the same smaller subproblems come up again and again, so solving each of them once saves a great deal of work. Chapter two showed the waste that overlap causes. The plain recursive Fibonacci function recomputes the same values over and over, and the script counts two hundred and forty-two thousand, seven hundred and eighty-five calls for fib of twenty-five. Adding a memo, a dictionary from input to answer, here provided by Python's cache decorator, means each distinct value of n is computed once and then looked up. The call count drops to twenty-six. The memory card shows the memo after computing fib of six: one entry per value of n, each depending only on the two below it. That picture is the real idea. Memoisation turns the exponential recursion tree into a small dependency graph with one node per distinct subproblem and edges to the subproblems it needs. That graph is a DAG, because a subproblem only ever depends on smaller ones, and the cost of the whole computation is roughly the number of nodes times the work per node. Every dynamic program in this chapter is built the same way. Define the subproblems, make sure they overlap and combine optimally, and solve each one once. The weighted dock slots that defeated the greedy rule are the first real example, in the next section.

The hardest and most important step in dynamic programming is choosing the state, and the discipline that helps most is to say in words exactly what each state means. Take Chapter eleven's weighted dock slots, extended here to seven, and sort them by finishing time. Define OPT of i as the best total value achievable using only the first i slots in that order. Define p of i as the number of slots that finish no later than slot i starts. Those are exactly the slots that are compatible with slot i and come before it. The script prints p for each slot. The base case is simple: with zero slots, the best value is zero. Now the recurrence. Consider the last of the first i slots, slot i. Any plan either leaves it out or includes it. If it is left out, the best possible is OPT of i minus one, by the definition of the state. If it is included, it contributes its value, and every other slot in the plan must be compatible with it, which means it must be among the first p of i slots. The best way to choose those is OPT of p of i. So OPT of i is the larger of OPT of i minus one, and the value of slot i plus OPT of p of i. That sentence is the whole algorithm. The recurrence is written as a comment in the code, which is a good habit. Correctness follows by induction on i. Every plan for the first i slots falls into exactly one of the two cases, and each case is solved optimally by smaller states, assuming those are correct. Notice what the state remembers that greedy did not: for every prefix, the best value, not just the slots chosen so far. That extra information is what lets the algorithm discover that a long valuable slot beats three short ones.

A recurrence can be evaluated in two ways, and the code on the board does both. The first is top-down, called memoisation. Write the recurrence directly as a recursive function, and cache every result. When the function asks for a smaller state, the recursion computes it if it has not been seen, or returns the cached answer if it has. The recursion discovers a valid order of evaluation by itself, and it only ever solves the states that are actually needed for the final answer. The cost is the call stack. A deep chain of dependencies needs one frame per level, which in Python can hit the recursion limit for large inputs. The second is bottom-up, called tabulation. Allocate a table with one entry per state, and fill it in an order where every state's dependencies are already computed before it is reached. Here, each OPT of i depends on OPT of i minus one and OPT of p of i, and p of i is always less than i, so simply filling the table in increasing order of i is valid. There is no recursion at all, and because the order is explicit, it is easy to see which earlier entries are still needed, which makes space reduction possible later. The table on the board compares the two. Both produce fifteen, and the printed table shows how the best value grows as slots are added: zero, two, four, six, ten, ten, thirteen, fifteen. The running time is the number of states times the work per state. There are n states, each needing constant work once p is known, so after the n log n sort and the binary searches for p, the dynamic program itself is linear. The most common mistake with tabulation is a wrong fill order, which reads entries before they are written. Always check the dependency direction first.

A filled table gives the best value, fifteen, but a dispatcher needs the actual plan: which slots to accept. Reconstruction recovers it by walking back through the table. Start at the last state, OPT of seven, and ask which side of the max produced it. Here, taking slot seven gives five plus OPT of five, which is fifteen, while leaving it out gives OPT of six, thirteen. So slot seven is in the plan, and the walk jumps to p of seven, the slots compatible with it. If the other side had produced the value, slot i would be left out, and the walk would move to i minus one. The table already contains everything needed, so no extra storage is required, although some programs store the choice made at each state to make this step trivial. Ties need attention. At i equals five, both sides of the max give ten: including slot five gives four plus six, and leaving it out gives OPT of four, also ten. Both continuations lead to optimal plans, and the tie rule decides which one is returned. The output shows both. Preferring to include slots on ties returns five short slots. Preferring to leave them out returns the long slot from two to nine plus the slot from twelve to fifteen. Both total fifteen. Neither is wrong, but they are different, and that matters if the caller expects a particular one, or compares results across runs. As chapter one insisted, the contract should say whether any optimal plan is acceptable, or which one is required. Finally, reconstruction is easy to get subtly wrong, so it deserves a check. Recompute the value of the returned plan directly from its slots, and confirm it equals OPT of n. The script prints that sum next to each plan.

Dynamic programming is especially natural for comparing two sequences, because the subproblems are pairs of prefixes. The first example is edit distance: the fewest single-letter edits, meaning insertions, deletions or replacements, that turn one string into another. It is how a system can suggest that a mistyped depot label probably meant a real one. The state D of i and j is the fewest edits that turn the first i letters of a into the first j letters of b. The boundaries are easy. Turning i letters into nothing takes i deletions, and turning nothing into j letters takes j insertions. For every other cell, consider the last letters of the two prefixes. We can delete a's last letter, costing one plus the cell above. We can insert b's last letter, costing one plus the cell to the left. Or we can match the two last letters, which is free if they are equal and costs one replacement if not, plus the cell diagonally above-left. The cell takes the minimum of the three. The output prints the whole table for depot and depart. The bottom-right cell is two: replace the O with an A, and insert an R. The second example is the longest common subsequence: the longest sequence of letters that appears in both strings in order, though not necessarily together. The state L of i and j is the length of the longest subsequence common to the two prefixes. When the last letters are equal, it extends the diagonal by one. Otherwise, it takes the better of dropping a letter from either string. Depot and depart share D, E, P, T, of length four, and reconstruction walks back through the table just as in the previous section. Both tables have about n times m cells with constant work each, so both run in time and space proportional to n times m.

The zero-one knapsack problem is the standard example of a capacity constraint. One van can carry ten kilograms, each parcel has a weight and a value, and each parcel is either taken whole or left behind. The goal is the greatest total value that fits. The first attempt at a state is usually the first i parcels, and it fails. Knowing only which parcels have been considered says nothing about how much room is left, so the recurrence cannot tell whether the next parcel still fits. The state must carry that information too. So K of i and c is the best value obtainable from the first i parcels when c kilograms of capacity are available. Parcel i is either skipped, leaving K of i minus one and c, or taken, if its weight w fits, giving its value plus K of i minus one and c minus w, the best from the earlier parcels in the remaining capacity. The table has one row per parcel and one column per kilogram of capacity. For the four parcels in the script, the best value is ninety, taking the four kilogram parcel worth forty and the three kilogram parcel worth fifty. On this small instance, taking the most valuable parcels first, or the lightest first, happens to reach ninety as well. But neither rule is safe in general. Each can fill the van badly on other instances, which is exactly why the exchange argument from chapter eleven has no counterpart for this problem. Reconstruction follows the same pattern as before. Wherever K of i and c differs from K of i minus one and c, parcel i was taken, and capacity is reduced by its weight. Subset sum is the yes or no question underneath: can some parcels weigh exactly nine kilograms? Keeping the set of sums reachable so far, and extending it one parcel at a time, answers it, and here the answer is yes.

A different family of dynamic programs works on ranges. The state is an interval, from i to j, and the recurrence chooses where to split it. The example merges adjacent batches of parcels into one consignment. Batches can only be merged with their immediate neighbours, and each merge costs the combined size of the two batches being merged. The order of merges matters, because large batches merged early get counted again in every later merge. The state cost of i and j is the cheapest way to merge batches i through j into a single batch. A single batch costs nothing. Otherwise, think about the very last merge. It combines two pieces, the batches from i to k, and the batches from k plus one to j, for some split point k. Those two pieces must each have been merged optimally, and the last merge always costs the total size of the range. So cost of i and j is the total from i to j, plus the minimum over every k of the two sub-costs. The script computes this for four batches and gets two hundred, and confirms it against brute force, which tries every possible merge order. There are about n squared over two intervals, and each tries up to n split points, so the cost is n cubed. The same shape solves many other problems, such as the best order to multiply a chain of matrices, or the best way to build a search tree from known access frequencies. The board ends with a unifying view. Every dynamic program is secretly a graph problem. Its states are vertices, its choices are weighted edges, and the dependency structure is a DAG. Finding the optimal answer is finding a shortest or longest path in that DAG, exactly as in chapter ten, and evaluating states in a valid order is processing the DAG in topological order.

The cost of a dynamic program can be read straight from its design: the number of states, times the work done per state. The knapsack table has n times C states with constant work each. The interval DP has about n squared states with up to n choices each, so it is cubic. Not every dynamic program is quadratic, and the only reliable way to know is to count. Space can often be reduced. Each row of the knapsack table depends only on the row before it, so a single array of C plus one cells is enough, overwritten as each parcel is processed. But the direction of the loop over capacities now matters a great deal, and the script shows why. Looping downward, from high capacity to low, each cell reads entries that still hold the previous row's values, and the answer is the correct ninety. Looping upward, a cell can read an entry already updated for the current parcel, which means the same parcel is taken again. The result is one hundred and fifty, three copies of the three kilogram parcel, which is the answer to a different problem, the unbounded knapsack. Space reduction also has a cost. Once old rows are overwritten, the plan can no longer be reconstructed, so keep the full table when the plan itself is needed. One limit remains, and it connects back to chapter two. The knapsack table has a column for every unit of capacity, so its size grows with the capacity's numeric value, not with the number of digits needed to write it. The script scales the capacity by a thousand. Its length grows from four bits to fourteen, a modest increase, but the table grows from fifty-five cells to over fifty thousand. Such an algorithm is called pseudopolynomial. It is polynomial in the value C, but exponential in the length of the input, which matters in the final chapter.

Every algorithm in this chapter compares symbols, so the first question is what a symbol actually is. Text has at least three different units, and they do not line up. At the bottom are bytes, which is what is stored and transmitted. The common UTF-8 encoding uses between one and four bytes for each code point. A code point is the next level up: one numbered entry in the Unicode standard, and it is what a Python string holds. The len function counts code points. At the top are graphemes, what a reader perceives as a single character. The script shows how far apart these can be. The word café can be written with a single precomposed e acute, or with a plain e followed by a combining accent mark. On screen the two look identical. But they are different sequences of code points, so Python reports that they are not equal, and their lengths are four and five. A search for one will not find the other, which is exactly the kind of silent failure chapter one warned about. Unicode defines normalisation forms to deal with this. Converting both strings to the composed form, called NFC, makes them equal, as the output shows. Case is another decision. Lowercasing is enough for depot names in plain English, but casefold is the more thorough comparison, and it correctly matches the German sharp s against a double s. None of these choices is universally right, so they belong in the contract of any text search: which normalisation is applied, and whether comparison ignores case. The algorithms in this chapter compare code points exactly as stored. Any normalisation is the caller's job, done once, before searching.

A trie is a tree organised by characters rather than by whole keys. The root represents the empty string. Each node maps a character to a child node, so every path from the root spells out a prefix, and a special marker on a node says that a complete stored word ends there. Words that share a prefix share the path that spells it. The board shows part of a trie built from depot labels. North, north east and north hub all begin with the same five letters, so they share one path for N, O, R, T, H, and only then branch, into E A S T and H U B. Naval shares only the first N. That sharing is what makes tries efficient for questions about prefixes. To find every label that starts with a given prefix, walk down from the root one character at a time. That costs time proportional to the length of the prefix, regardless of how many labels are stored. Then collect every complete word in the subtree below. The demo asks for labels starting with north and gets all three, and labels starting with E A, which gives east and east port. If any character of the prefix is missing along the way, the search stops immediately with no results, as it does for south. Tries also involve a representation choice. This version uses a Python dict at each node, which handles any alphabet but costs memory for every node. Here the trie has twenty-five nodes for thirty-nine letters of labels, so the sharing saved some space. For a small, fixed alphabet, such as digits, an array of children per node is faster and more compact. Tries answer prefix questions. They are not a general substring search, which the next sections take up.

The basic text search problem is to find every position where a pattern of length m occurs in a text of length n, such as every occurrence of port in a list of route codes. The naive algorithm does exactly what the problem says. It tries each starting position in the text in turn, compares the pattern character by character, and stops at the first mismatch.
