If all m characters match, it reports that start. One detail in the specification deserves attention: occurrences can overlap. In the text A B A B A B A, the pattern A B A occurs at positions zero, two and four, and the occurrences at zero and two share a letter. The table on the board traces each window. The naive algorithm finds overlapping occurrences naturally, because it tries every start independently. In practice the naive algorithm is often fast, because on ordinary text most windows fail on the first or second character. But its worst case is poor, and it is easy to trigger. Let the text be a thousand A's, and the pattern ninety-nine A's followed by a B. At every one of the nine hundred and one starting positions, the first ninety-nine characters match, and only the hundredth fails. The script counts ninety thousand one hundred comparisons. In general, the worst case is n times m. The waste has a clear cause. After matching ninety-nine characters at one position, the algorithm moves one place to the right and starts comparing from scratch, even though it has just read almost all of the characters it is about to read again. It forgets what the partial match told it. The next section shows how to remember.

The Knuth Morris Pratt algorithm, KMP for short, removes the waste by remembering what a partial match proved. Its key ingredient is the prefix function of the pattern, computed once before the search. For each position i, pi of i is the length of the longest proper prefix of the pattern, up to and including i, that is also a suffix of it. Such a prefix and suffix pair is called a border. It is worth reading the table on the board slowly. For the pattern A B A B A C, the prefix A B A B A ends with A B A, which is also how it starts, so pi at that position is three. The full pattern, ending in C, has no border at all, so its entry is zero. Here is why that helps. Suppose the search has matched k characters of the pattern and then hits a mismatch. Those k matched characters are known exactly: they are the first k characters of the pattern. The longest border of that prefix tells us how much of it can serve as the start of the next possible match. So instead of moving back in the text, KMP keeps its place in the text and falls back in the pattern to position pi of k minus one, and tries again. No character of the text is ever read twice for the same purpose. After a complete match it falls back the same way, which is how overlapping occurrences are found, as the output shows for A B A in A B A B A B A. Building pi costs time proportional to m, and the scan costs time proportional to n, so KMP is linear, n plus m, even in the worst case. On the input that cost the naive algorithm ninety thousand one hundred comparisons, KMP takes one thousand nine hundred and one steps.

A different approach to text search compares numbers instead of strings. The Rabin Karp algorithm computes a hash of the pattern, and a hash of every window of m characters in the text. A match is only possible where the two hashes agree, and comparing two numbers is much cheaper than comparing two strings. The trick that makes it fast is a rolling hash. The hash treats the window as a number written in a large base, reduced modulo M. Moving the window one place to the right means removing the outgoing character's contribution and adding the incoming one, which takes constant time, rather than rehashing all m characters. The crucial point is that equal hashes do not mean equal strings. Many different windows share each hash value, so collisions are not a theoretical risk. They will happen. The script makes this deliberately obvious by using a tiny modulus of eleven. Searching a route string for port, the correct version, which verifies each candidate by comparing the actual characters, finds the three real occurrences, and counts four false alarms where the hash matched but the text did not. The careless version, which trusts the hash alone, reports seven matches, four of them wrong. In practice, the modulus is a large prime, ideally chosen at random, which makes collisions rare, and with verification the expected running time is linear. But rare is not never, and an adversary who knows the modulus can construct collisions on purpose, just as with the hash tables of chapter five. So the rule is the same as there. A hash can quickly rule a candidate out. It can never, by itself, prove two strings equal. Rolling hashes are especially useful for searching many patterns at once, or for finding repeated blocks in long texts.

KMP and rolling hashes preprocess the pattern and then scan the whole text. When the same text will be searched for many different patterns, such as a long log searched over and over, it pays to preprocess the text instead. A suffix array is the standard structure for that. Take every suffix of the text, the text from each position to the end, and list their starting positions in sorted order of the suffixes. For banana, the sorted suffixes are A, A N A, A N A N A, banana, N A, and N A N A, so the suffix array is five, three, one, zero, four, two. The key observation is that every occurrence of a pattern is the beginning of some suffix. And in sorted order, all the suffixes that begin with the same pattern sit next to each other. So the occurrences of a pattern form one contiguous block of the suffix array, as the board shows for A N A, at positions one and three. Finding that block is a binary search over the sorted suffixes, which needs about log n comparisons, each comparing up to m characters, so a query costs m log n regardless of how many times the text is searched. The output also prints the LCP array, the length of the longest common prefix between each suffix and the one before it in sorted order. Large values reveal repeated substrings. The largest here is three, for the repeat A N A. LCP values support many further queries, such as finding the longest repeated substring, directly. One honest limit. The example builds the array by simply sorting suffixes, which is easy to read but slow, because comparing suffixes can take long. There are much faster constructions, including linear-time ones, which are beyond the scope of this course.

This chapter has introduced several tools, and they answer different questions at different costs, so the choice should follow the workload. The table on the board summarises it. For a single search in a modest amount of text, use the built-in string find method or the in operator. For a guaranteed linear worst case, use KMP, which never rescans the text. When one fixed text will be searched for many different patterns, preprocess the text into a suffix array, and answer each query in m log n. When the questions are about prefixes of a set of words, such as completing a depot name as it is typed, use a trie. And rolling hashes suit finding repeated or near-duplicate blocks. It is important to understand the boundary between these teaching algorithms and Python's library. CPython's own string search is not the KMP shown in this chapter. It uses its own optimised method, written in C. The script times them on the same text, and the card shows one recorded run, labelled as such. The built-in search took about twenty microseconds, and the hand-written KMP about three milliseconds, more than a hundred times slower. That gap is not a verdict on KMP's algorithm, which has an excellent guarantee. It reflects interpreted Python loops against compiled code, a constant factor of exactly the kind chapter two warned about. The practical lesson is to use the library for production text search, and to understand these algorithms so you know what guarantees exist, when to need them, and how to reason about cost. Whatever tool is chosen, state the assumptions in the contract: the alphabet, the normalisation form, whether comparison ignores case, and whether overlapping occurrences count.

This final chapter asks a different kind of question. Not how to solve a problem quickly, but whether a fast exact algorithm is likely to exist at all, and what to do when it is not. The theory behind that question is stated for decision problems, so the first step is to see how ordinary problems become yes or no questions. Take loading a van. As an optimisation problem, it asks for the heaviest load that fits within nine thousand grams, and the answer is eight thousand seven hundred. As a decision problem, it asks: is there a load of at least k grams that fits? For eight thousand seven hundred the answer is yes, and for eight thousand eight hundred it is no. The two forms are closely linked. Given a fast decision procedure, a binary search over k finds the optimum, and the script recovers eight thousand seven hundred from fourteen decision calls. Conversely, the optimum answers every decision at once. So, for problems like this one, the two forms are equally hard, up to a polynomial factor. Decisions are used because a yes answer can come with a certificate, a piece of evidence that can be checked, which section three builds on. One more point from earlier chapters returns here, the encoding of the input. Complexity theory measures input size in the number of bits needed to write the input down. Chapter two showed trial division being exponential in the number of digits, and chapter twelve showed the knapsack table growing with the numeric value of the capacity. Writing a capacity in binary takes only its number of bits, so a table indexed by the capacity itself is exponential in the input size. Whenever a claim about efficient algorithms is made, it is with respect to this encoding.

The central tool for comparing problems is the reduction. A reduction from problem A to problem B is a procedure that transforms any instance of A into an instance of B with exactly the same answer, and does so in polynomial time. If such a reduction exists, then any fast algorithm for B immediately gives a fast algorithm for A: transform the instance, then solve it with B's algorithm. In other words, B is at least as hard as A. The script gives a concrete example. Subset sum asks whether some of the numbers add up exactly to a target t. Partition asks whether a set of numbers can be split into two halves with equal sums. The reduction takes a subset sum instance with total s, and adds two new numbers to it: s plus t, and two s minus t. The new total is four s, so an even split needs two s on each side. The two added numbers cannot be on the same side, since together they already make three s. So whichever side holds two s minus t must be completed by original numbers summing to exactly t. An even split exists exactly when a subset sums to t. The output checks this for three targets, and the direct answer and the answer via partition agree every time. The most important thing about reductions is their direction, and it is easy to get backwards. To show that a new problem is hard, reduce a problem already known to be hard to the new one. That shows the new problem is at least as hard. Reducing the new problem to a known hard problem shows only that it is no harder, which says nothing at all about whether it is difficult. Easy problems reduce to hard ones all the time.

Reductions organise problems into classes, and the names are worth getting exactly right. P is the class of decision problems that can be solved in polynomial time. Every problem in chapters three to thirteen with a polynomial algorithm, such as shortest paths or sorting stated as a decision, belongs to P. NP is the class of decision problems where a yes answer comes with a certificate that can be checked in polynomial time. The script shows the difference between checking and finding. It has twenty-two parcel weights and asks whether some of them sum to exactly fifty thousand. Given a certificate, a list of eight chosen weights, checking it takes eight additions and a comparison. Finding one, in the worst case, may mean searching through two to the twenty-two subsets, over four million. A problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it, so it is at least as hard as anything in NP. A problem is NP-complete if it is both in NP and NP-hard. Subset sum and partition are NP-complete, and so is the decision version of the delivery tour problem. The table on the board collects these definitions. The most famous open question in computer science is whether P equals NP: whether every problem whose solutions can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly. It is unresolved. Nobody has found a polynomial algorithm for any NP-complete problem, and nobody has proved that none exists. Two misunderstandings are common. NP does not stand for not polynomial. And NP-hard does not mean that every instance is hard. It is a statement about the worst case. Many real instances are small, or structured, or have small numbers, and are solved exactly every day, as the knapsack DP of chapter twelve was.

When a problem is NP-hard and the instances are large, insisting on the exact optimum may mean waiting forever. The alternative is to accept an answer that is not quite optimal, but to be precise about how far from optimal it might be. The delivery tour is the natural example. A van must visit every depot once and return to the hub, travelling as little as possible. This is the travelling salesperson problem, and it is NP-hard. With six depots besides the hub there are seven hundred and twenty possible orders, few enough to try them all, and the shortest tour is twenty-eight point six kilometres. The nearest neighbour heuristic is much faster. It always drives to the closest depot not yet visited. On this map it produces a tour of thirty-six point eight kilometres, one point two nine times the optimum. The plot shows both tours. You can see where nearest neighbour went wrong: it greedily took nearby depots early, and was left with a long drive at the end. It is important to separate two kinds of claim. An approximation algorithm comes with a proof that, on every instance, its answer is within a stated factor of the optimum. A heuristic comes with no such proof. Its quality is only observed, as here, on particular instances. Nearest neighbour is a heuristic, and on some carefully built inputs its tours can be arbitrarily worse than optimal. So the ratio of one point two nine is evidence about this map, not a guarantee about the next one. The honest practice is to use both. Measure a heuristic against exact answers on instances small enough to solve exactly, report the observed ratios as evidence, and prefer methods with proven guarantees when a bound must hold.

Randomness has appeared several times in this course: random pivots in quicksort, random seeds for hash tables. This section states precisely what randomisation buys. There are two kinds of randomised algorithm. A Las Vegas algorithm always gives the correct answer, but its running time depends on its random choices. Quicksort and quickselect with random pivots are Las Vegas, with expected n log n and expected linear time. A Monte Carlo algorithm runs in a fixed time, but its answer is only correct with high probability. The script is a Monte Carlo example from the depot. Has the scanner seen exactly the same parcels as the manifest, perhaps in a different order? Sorting both lists would answer it in n log n. Instead, the algorithm computes a fingerprint of each list: the product of x minus each value, modulo a large prime P, at a randomly chosen x. If the lists contain the same parcels, the fingerprints are always equal. If they differ, the two products are different polynomials, and they can agree at no more than n points, so the chance of a random x fooling the check is at most n over P. The error is one-sided. A different answer is always right. A same answer can be wrong, with small probability. Independent trials drive that probability down quickly, because each one multiplies it. Here a single trial errs with probability at most one in a thousand, and three trials push it below one in a billion, far less likely than a hardware fault during the run. The output shows the check accepting the reversed list and rejecting the list with one parcel replaced. And as chapter two stressed, the randomness belongs to the algorithm. No particular input is bad for it, because an adversary cannot choose the random x.

Every algorithm so far could see its whole input before deciding anything. Many real decisions cannot wait. They must be made now, with the future unknown. Such problems are called online, and they have a limit of their own, which no amount of computing power removes. The classic example is renting or buying. The depot needs an extra van for an unknown number of days. Renting costs one per day, and buying costs ten, once. Each morning, the planner learns only whether the van is needed again today. With hindsight, the decision is easy. An offline algorithm that knows the total number of days simply rents if it is fewer than ten, and buys on the first day otherwise, paying the smaller of the days and ten. The online rule cannot know. A good rule is to rent until the rental total would reach the purchase price, and then buy. The output and the plot compare the two. For short needs, both pay the same. For ten days or more, the online rule pays nineteen, nine days of rent and then the purchase, while the offline optimum pays ten. The ratio never exceeds one point nine, which is two minus one over B. It can also be shown that no deterministic online rule has a better worst-case ratio for this problem. This style of analysis is called competitive analysis. An online algorithm is compared, in the worst case, with an opponent who knows the future, and its competitive ratio is the factor it might lose. The limit here is different in kind from NP-hardness. The online rule runs instantly. What it lacks is information. Even with unlimited time, no rule could match the offline optimum on every sequence, because the information needed to do so has not arrived yet.

This section returns to a question from chapter three, because it shows the theme of the whole course in a small space: the operations a program needs decide the structure it should use. Chapter three's prefix sums answer any range total, such as the grams dispatched between hours three and five, with a single subtraction, after one linear pass to build them. But they assume the data never changes. The script corrects one hour's figure after the prefix sums were built, and the static answer is now stale, still seventy-five hundred, because every later prefix would need rebuilding, a linear cost per update. When updates and queries are mixed, a Fenwick tree, also called a binary indexed tree, supports both in logarithmic time. Each cell of its array covers a block of positions whose size is the lowest set bit of the cell's index. An update adds to the cells whose blocks contain the position, found by repeatedly adding the lowest set bit. A prefix query sums cells whose blocks tile the prefix, found by repeatedly removing it. Each walks only about log n cells. The output shows the Fenwick tree giving seventy-five hundred, and then eight thousand two hundred after the correction. A segment tree is the more general tool. It stores a node for every range produced by repeatedly halving the array, so any query range can be assembled from about log n nodes, and an update changes one path. Unlike a Fenwick tree, which needs an operation that can be undone, such as subtraction, a segment tree works with any associative operation, such as minimum or maximum, at the cost of more memory and code. The table compares all three, and the choice comes down to whether the data changes, and which aggregate is needed.

Before the final synthesis, it is worth being explicit about the boundaries of this course, as the plan promised at the start. The course has covered the foundations: the main data structures, sequences, hash tables, trees, heaps and graphs. The main design techniques: searching and sorting, exhaustive search with pruning, greedy algorithms, dynamic programming and string matching. And the reasoning that ties them together: contracts, invariants, cost bounds, and the assumptions every claim depends on. Several important areas were deliberately left out, because each needs a course of its own to do properly. Network flow and matching, which solve assignment and capacity problems on graphs. Computational geometry, for problems about points, lines and shapes. The fast Fourier transform and numerical methods, where floating point behaviour becomes central. The number theory behind cryptography. Parallel and distributed algorithms, where many processors cooperate and communication is the real cost. Persistent and succinct data structures, which keep old versions or use nearly minimal space. And the large catalogues of patterns used in programming contests. The board lists them beside what was covered. Each of these has its own models of cost, its own proof techniques, and its own body of practice, and none can be learned well from a single section. What does carry over is the set of habits this course has practised in every chapter. Specify the problem before solving it. Prove that the solution meets its contract. Analyse its cost under a stated model. Measure to check the analysis. And always state the limits of what has been shown. Those habits apply equally well in every one of these directions.

The course ends where it began, with the delivery planner, now assembled from every chapter. The final skill is to bring the pieces together into one design, and to write the reasoning down. A good format for that is a decision record: for each part of the problem, the choice made, and the evidence behind it. The board maps the planner part by part. Looking up a parcel by identifier uses a hash map, from chapter five, with expected constant time under a stated hashing assumption. The queue of urgent parcels uses a heap, from chapter seven. Travel times between depots use Dijkstra's algorithm, from chapter ten, which is valid because driving minutes are never negative. Loading each van is a knapsack problem, which is NP-hard in general, but chapter twelve's dynamic program solves it exactly here, because a capacity of nine thousand grams makes the table small. That is the pseudopolynomial limit working in our favour. Planning each van's tour is also NP-hard, and the instances are too large to search, so the record chooses a heuristic, and states that it was measured against exact answers on small instances, with no guarantee claimed. The script prints the record itself. Every line pairs a choice with its justification, and the last line states the limits plainly: no live traffic data, and tours not proven optimal. That honesty is part of the design, not an afterthought. The order of work throughout has always been the same, and it is worth repeating one last time. First a correct algorithm, with its contract and proof. Then its cost, under a stated model. Only then benchmarks, to check the analysis and choose between correct candidates. Completing this course is a start, not mastery. Practical skill comes from applying these habits, getting feedback, and practising on problems of your own.
